data.title: The rise and fall of British helicopters
data.description:
Do you have a favourite helicopter? Mine, as a child, was Airwolf. But it could have been the helicopter that dropped Anneka Rice off at so many castles in the pioneering 1980s Channel 4 game-show Treasure Hunt, or the Blue Thunder choppers that ferry our elite SAS teams around Britain, tackling emergencies.

Today, in addition to their use by armed forces, they are status symbols for the 0.01 per cent. Donald Trump used to owned a fleet of three Sikorsky S-76 helicopters, with predictably gilded interiors. Yet not so long ago, some believed this form of transport would be used regularly by the hoi polloi; hopping into a chopper would be as common as hailing a black cab.

This month marks 40 years since the demise of British Airways Helicopters, and that brief moment in time when it seemed scheduled passenger helicopter services might actually catch on. So why did the helicopter never go truly mainstream?

Up in the Airlink

Focke-Wulf’s FW61 was unveiled in the 1930s, before Russian-American pioneer Igor Sikorsky took up the baton in the 1940s. The US company he founded would go on to dominate these machines’ development for half a century.

But passenger helicopter services actually began in the UK. The route? From Liverpool to Cardiff, launched by BEA in 1950, with an intriguing stop in Wrexham that would have suited Rob McElhenney and Ryan Reynolds if it were operating today.

More BEA routes followed, such as Birmingham to Northolt, and on to Heathrow. Birmingham got a pioneering “Rotorstation” for helicopters to land at. It was opened at Heybarnes Recreation Ground in Hay Mills – Peaky Blinders territory. Three flights left for London daily.

Between 1978 and 1986, a helicopter shuttle service, dubbed the Airlink, connected Gatwick and Heathrow. This was before the M25 was finished and when the journey between the two main London airports was tortuous. Helicopters ferried transit passengers from apron to apron in minutes.

A vision of the future

The thinking among many was that helicopters would be omnipresent. During the Festival of Britain, there was a helicopter landing pad on the Southbank in London. The Southbank was earmarked for a more permanent heliport, which explains the brutalist design of the Queen Elizabeth Hall. It was supposed to protect against the noise and vibrations of helicopters.

In the end a heliport at Battersea was opened, further along the River Thames, and is still in use today. Architects’ designs for Sixties new towns always showed two things: a monorail, and helicopters fluttering in the sky. This was the vision of the future – back when we believed in a future that would be better.

Even the GPO became enamoured with helicopters and trialled their use to deliver post to the rural towns of Norfolk. Quite what Farmer Giles, drinking a pint of warm Bullard’s outside The Railway Inn in Docking on a Sunday afternoon in 1948, would have made of the sight of a GPO Sikorsky S-51 on a post run to Wells-Next-The-Sea is anyone’s guess.

In the Fifties, Britain ramped up its own helicopter production at Westland’s Yeovil site, which became the home of the British helicopter. The Dragonfly, Widgeon, Whirlwind and Wessex became instantly recognisable machines built in Somerset. The Sea King, Wasp and Scout followed, then it was into the era of more modern machines like the Puma, Gazelle and Lynx.

Away with the Faireys

Among the more bizarre ideas was the Fairey Rotodyne: a hybrid between a plane and a helicopter that doesn’t look a million miles away from the stretched fuselage of the Chinook. In 1959 it flew from Heathrow to Paris via Dover and Brussels, but it wouldn’t catch on. One of the problems was the immense noise its rotors generated. This was going to be a problem when it was clattering over the roofs of densely populated areas of South London on the way to Battersea Heliport.

Westland took over Fairey in the 1960s, but domestic helicopter production was to become a hot political potato. Britain’s varied and incredibly successful aerospace entities were walking a tightrope between innovating, investing, exporting and balancing the books. Their designs were legendary, but of course not everything worked. There was always a tussle between nationalising everything into what would become British Aerospace and selling parts off to foreign investors.

Westland became a political football during the so-called Westland Affair in 1985, which pitted different factions of Margaret Thatcher’s Conservative government against each other, as arguments raged over whether to maintain this facility in Yeovil, who should run it and who would pay for it.

End of an era

Why did helicopters fade away? As with other futuristic transport ideas like hovertrains, monorails, hovercraft and other “gadgetbahns”, their relatively high cost and niggling technical problems could never be fully resolved.

Aeroplanes, trains and cars driving on motorways won the transport arms race because they could be easily scaled, and eventually mass uptake drastically reduced costs. These forms of transport made money rather than costing it.

Motorways connect us. With the M40 complete, there was no need to take a helicopter from Birmingham to London. Helicopters are also gas guzzlers – even Porsche owners would baulk at the price of a full tank. Sabena wanted to follow the Rotodyne’s first international flight and start a helicopter from London to Brussels – but Eurostar does that journey more efficiently.

In the US, where traffic is terrible and public transport is worse, Blade has put up a fight, offering relatively affordable flights from JFK to Manhattan, but without the drama of the former Pan Am helicopter, which whisked passengers to the top of the Pan Am HQ in Midtown in the 1960s.

Helicopters are still popular as niche forms of transport, and incredibly useful for medical evacuations, police and military use, and VIP transport. UK Air Sea Rescue has used helicopters to rescue the lives of countless sailors around our shores, and helicopters have ferried thousands of workers to oil and gas rigs in the North Sea and beyond, from Aberdeen, Norwich, Humberside and other hubs.

But their mass-market use has dwindled in the face of competition – which is sad, because they have a real value. The experience of being in one is not like regular flying because you’re so low you can see everything below you. The feeling of rising into the sky for the first time is surreal.

Rare survivors

The Scilly Isles are one of the rare examples of a route where helicopters make sense, and these flights have continued on and off from 1964 to this day. My honeymooning parents cannot have been the only holidaymakers caught out by rough seas who needed to use the helicopter as a way to swiftly get off the islands. For locals, they are a lifeline back to the shops, schools and health services of Penzance. This is now the last surviving scheduled British helicopter service.

Nice to Monaco and Saint-Tropez are other popular services going strong, as are Helity’s routes from Malaga and Algeciras to the headline-grabbing Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Hong Kong to Macau is another example. Faroese flag carrier Atlantic Airways runs domestic helicopter flights. But anyone who’s gone puffin-spotting in Mykines, and found themselves stuck on the island for days due to bad weather, will know that helicopters aren’t much use in storms or low visibility, which is pretty much every day in a Faroe Islands winter.

For the super-rich class there will always be helicopters ready to take them to the British Grand Prix or Goodwood (two of the biggest weekends for the Battersea Heliport). But for the rest of us, the dream of flying everywhere by helicopter is elusive. It’s not impossible though – this is why helicopter aficionados specifically head to Tresco or Tórshavn.

data.title: Netherlands brought to standstill after train sabotage
data.description:
The Netherlands has been brought to a standstill after a sabotage attack on the rail network.

Pipes and cables were found attached to rails at more than 20 locations, halting services across much of the country and disrupting trains to Amsterdam’s Schiphol international airport.

Around midday fires erupted alongside several highways, forcing authorities to close roads.

Farmers admitted starting the fires by setting hay bales and cars alight in protest at the government’s budget which they said would increase their costs and threaten the viability of their businesses.

But the Farmers Defence Force (FDF) said the radical activist group was not responsible for the railway sabotage although it could not rule out some landowners had acted individually.

“We feel like the country is on fire. Farmers feel as though their businesses are on fire because of the government’s plans,” said Sieta van Keimpema, a spokesman for the FDF.

Commenting on the damage to the railway, Joke van der Cruysen, a ProRail spokesman, said: “We discovered materials that had been deliberately placed there. We are therefore now classifying this as ‌sabotage ‌of the railway infrastructure.”

In a statement, Dutch police said: “Objects were found on railway tracks at several locations across the country, causing major disruption to rail traffic.”

They said officers remained at the affected sites but were working with ProRail to reopen the lines as quickly as possible.

A criminal investigation has been launched by police and AIVD, the Dutch intelligence agency.

Thousands of people were expected to travel to The Hague on Tuesday to watch the royal family ride through the city in horse-drawn carriages before King Willem-Alexander opened a new session of parliament.

He gave a speech outlining the government’s budget plans for 2027, which attracted criticism from farmers who claimed they were being unfairly blamed for nitrogen pollution.

They say the new rules aimed at reducing pollution from livestock could force them to cut herd sizes and they also fear being forced to sell their farms under a government buyout scheme.

In his speech, written by Rob Jetten, the prime minister, the King said it would be “irresponsible” not to tackle the nitrogen issue, even though this ​could hurt farmers.

Six people were arrested after throwing red paint along the procession route.

Tuesday’s rail attack is the latest in a series of sabotage incidents across Europe.

On Friday evening 44 people were injured when a train derailed near Cléon in Normandy after hitting a large section of rail left on the track.

“The reasons for its presence are unknown and will have to be determined by the investigation,” said Sébastien Gallois, the public prosecutor of Rouen.

There have been a number of other sabotage incidents across Europe this year, including a spate of attacks on Germany’s electricity grid.

Police have arrested a 48-year-old man on suspicion of the attacks in Brandenburg, Saxony and North Rhine-Westphalia.

data.title: Humanity running out of time, warns AI researcher
data.description:
An AI researcher has warned that “we might be running out of time” to prevent human extinction, months after quitting Google.

Bilal Chughtai, who was a London-based researcher at Google DeepMind, said in a post on X: “I too am extremely concerned by the default trajectory of this technology.

“I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome.”

His warning is the latest from experts about the risks AI may pose to humanity. Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, quit last week with a warning that AI systems were spiralling out of control.

Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, called for a slowdown in AI development over the weekend, saying the major companies needed to collaborate on “pacing” development.

Mr Chughtai, an AI safety researcher who joined DeepMind last year, wrote: “I think it’s possible that the AI companies might, in the next few years, succeed in building superintelligent AI systems that far exceed human capabilities in every domain. I am not confident that these AI systems will do what we want.

“Our present understanding of how to train AI systems that deeply want what we want is extremely rudimentary. Worse, we are not on track to solve alignment in time: frontier AI capabilities are improving much faster than our understanding of AI alignment.”

Mr Chugtai left Google in July, before it emerged that a rogue swarm of AI agents created by OpenAI had escaped their test environment to hack the tech company Hugging Face. The incident has been cited by many AI safety researchers as a potential turning point for AI risks.

Donald Trump dismissed fears about AI on Monday, calling them a “hoax” and claiming there was a “sick conspiracy” against the technology.

Louise Haigh, the First Secretary of State, will say on Tuesday that ministers must “heed the warnings” from tech companies about AI and that the Government must be “ready to work with international partners” on safety.

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, told LBC: “I don’t want people again to think anyone in the UK is naive about these risks, but I don’t want them to be overly worried as well.”

He added that Britain’s AI Security Institute, which tests models before they are released to the public “needs access to these things”.

Anthropic did not share its powerful Mythos 5.1 model with the taxpayer-backed body, reportedly under pressure from the Trump administration.

data.title: Britain to build turbines for Rolls-Royce mini-nuclear reactors
data.description:
British workers will build steam turbines for Rolls-Royce’s fleet of mini-nuclear reactors in a boost to domestic manufacturing.

Siemens Energy will produce the huge machines for a new generation of small modular reactors (SMRs) at its factory in Newcastle.

They will be used in the three Rolls-designed SMRs that are being built in Anglesey, as well as further reactors set to be built in the Czech Republic and Sweden.

It will be the first time large steam turbines have been made domestically in more than 20 years.

The expansion will follow an investment in the Newcastle factory understood to be worth tens of millions of pounds. It is expected to create 550 jobs.

It follows concerns raised by MPs that SMR components were set to be built abroad.

Rolls-Royce SMR said the decision by German engineering giant Siemens demonstrated how the company was “delivering its commitment to localisation, driving investment and re-shoring work that would have taken place overseas”.

Rolls-Royce SMR is an independent company, majority owned by Rolls-Royce but with investors including Qatar and France’s Perrodo family.

Chris Cholerton, the company’s chief executive, said: “We are building on a remarkable industrial legacy while creating and sustaining the skills and supply chain needed to deliver clean, secure and affordable energy for decades to come.”

Darren Davidson, of Siemens Energy, added: “We’re preparing to manufacture the next generation of steam turbines for small modular reactors, supporting energy security, creating skilled jobs and helping power the UK’s future energy mix.”

The Government awarded Rolls a contract to design and develop Britain’s first three SMRs last year.

They will be built in Anglesey, North Wales, in a project aimed at proving the commercial viability of the still-nascent technology by the mid-2030s. Each one will generate 470 megawatts of power.

Rolls selected Siemens Energy as its supplier of steam turbines last year, but there had been uncertainty about where the key components would be manufactured until now.

The British company faced a backlash earlier this year after it emerged that some other parts would be made overseas, including reactor pressure vessels that will be imported from either South Korea or the Czech Republic.

Labour ministers have set a target for 70pc of components to be made in Britain, and on Thursday they hailed the announcement by Siemens as proof their plan to “reindustrialise Britain” was working.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, said: “Producing these components here in the UK will help strengthen our energy security, reduce our exposure to volatile international gas markets, create new export opportunities for British industry, and reindustrialise the UK.”

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, added: “Building small modular reactors here in the UK presents huge benefits for us, from more export opportunities to more jobs on the ground at home.”

The Newcastle factory is expected to make both high-pressure turbines and valve casings.

It will also become the service hub for the turbines in the Rolls SMR fleet, ensuring a pipeline of work for the site that is expected to last decades.

The historic Parsons Works is the site once run by Sir Charles Parsons, the revered British engineer who helped to revolutionise marine propulsion with his invention of the multi-stage steam turbine.

It was established in 1889 and was where the steam turbine for Calder Hall – the world’s first commercial nuclear power station, in Cumbria – was built.

Grid-scale steam turbines have not been manufactured in the UK since the early 2000s, when Siemens scaled back its operations in Newcastle.

A steam turbine for a nuclear power plant has not been built in Britain since the early 1990s when one was supplied for the Sizewell B plant in Suffolk.

Tom Greatrex, of the Nuclear Industry Association, said: “This is what reindustrialisation looks like: a vital clean energy project reviving our old manufacturing capabilities to provide good, skilled jobs where we need them.

“The announcement is a real vote of confidence in industrial Britain and shows what SMRs and nuclear projects can deliver for this country.”

data.title: Jaguar Land Rover to axe 4,000 jobs
data.description:
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has confirmed plans to cut 4,000 jobs as its battles against competition from low-cost Chinese rivals and the shift to electric vehicles.

The company said on Monday that it would make the cuts over the next two years amid “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”.

Bosses insisted the move was necessary “to build a stronger, more competitive JLR”, as they targeted £1.7bn of savings from a wider overhaul of the business.

PB Balaji, the carmaker’s chief executive, added: “We recognise this will be difficult news for colleagues affected, and are committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect.”

The cuts represent a major setback to Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain.

It is understood they will largely fall on white-collar, salaried workers across JLR’s UK business and will not affect employees working in car production.

Some staff working in the manufacturer’s overseas divisions are also expected to be given the opportunity to take voluntary redundancy, which could reduce the effect on the British business.

Around 30,000 of the company’s 44,000 employees are based in the UK.

JLR’s global headquarters are in Coventry, while it operates major factories in manufacturing sites in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Merseyside.

No state bailout

MPs have warned that the cuts will have a “devastating” effect, with Mr Balaji set to hold a meeting with ministers and union officials on Tuesday.

He will sit down with Sharon Graham, the general secretary of Unite the Union, and Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, who has already made clear that there will be no money for a bailout of the company to protect jobs.

However, Mr Reynolds appeared to leave the door open for the Government to offer other forms of support.

“If it’s about long-term investment in the future, we do invest alongside industry on that,” he told Laura Kuenssberg’s Sunday morning BBC TV show.

At Tuesday’s meeting, Mr Balaji is expected to bring up the Government’s electric vehicle mandate – which could be watered down under changes being considered by ministers – as well as general pressures on the business, such as high energy costs and taxes on employment.

However, a source close to the company acknowledged that although improving conditions in the UK would help, JLR’s troubles were global in nature and echoed those of European giants, such as Volkswagen and Stellantis.

JLR, owned by Indian conglomerate Tata, is under pressure to shore up its finances amid rising costs and a slump in sales.

Revenues fell by almost 10pc in the first quarter, while pre-tax profits dropped by two thirds to £109m.

The carmaker, whose largest market is North America, has been rocked by Donald Trump’s 10pc tariff on vehicle imports to the US.

It is also still reeling from a crippling cyber attack that shut down production for more than a month and is estimated to have cost the company £1.9bn.

Further supply chain disruption and tough competition from cut-price Chinese rivals have also taken a toll.

Mr Balaji said the company was investing at least £15bn in electrification overall while it also seeks to make £1.7bn of savings.

Union officials are pushing for those who are losing their jobs to be retrained, potentially with support from the Government.

Unite’s Ms Graham said: “While the cuts planned are not expected to impact the UK manufacturing footprint, we need to ensure that the company is doing all it can to avoid unnecessary job losses amongst its highly skilled white collar workers.

“JLR’s vague statement today was not helpful and has only created increased uncertainty.

“Once again Unite will leave no stone unturned to support JLR workers. It cannot be acceptable that workers again are made to pay the price.”

She added that the union supported changes to the zero-emission vehicle mandate, which along with high energy costs had been “crippling the industry”.

A spokesman for Andy Burnham said on Monday that the Government remained “in close contact” with JLR.

They added: “We understand that this will be an uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and the wider communities.”

data.title: Crispin Odey loses battle over lifetime City ban
data.description:
Crispin Odey has failed to overturn a lifetime City ban after a series of sexual misconduct allegations.

The former hedge fund star lost his appeal against the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) on Monday, which banned him from the financial services sector last year.

The FCA had ruled that Mr Odey showed a “lack of integrity” after trying to hamper an internal investigation into misconduct allegations at his hedge fund Odey Asset Management (OAM). He denies the misconduct allegations.

Mr Odey received a final written warning from OAM in February 2021 “in relation to inappropriate behaviour” following an internal investigation.

The FCA said he then hampered an internal disciplinary process by dismissing two executive committees, which were due to hold disciplinary hearings.

In their decision dismissing Mr Odey’s appeal on Monday, the Upper Tribunal judges said: “He demonstrated a disregard for standards and requirements that he was reasonably expected to meet based upon the circumstances in question.

“He sees nothing wrong with his approach, and indeed he wrongly sees himself as the victim of both OAM’s actions and the FCA’s. As he put it in his evidence, he considers that he ‘was the victim in all this’.”

In a statement after the judgment, the FCA said Mr Odey’s only purpose “was self-preservation and to avoid being held to account for his behaviour”.

The City watchdog added: “He abused his power and disregarded the impact that his actions had on the firm and its employees – in particular women who had to work in a culture where his inappropriate behaviour had been normalised – in sending a clear message that he was effectively untouchable.”

The Upper Tribunal, which handles appeals against FCA decisions, also ruled that Mr Odey would face a fine of £1.53m alongside the ban, reduced from an initial proposition by the FCA of £1.83m.

Therese Chambers, the executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said on Monday: “Mr Odey clearly thought he could act with impunity.

“He twice sacked those tasked with protecting female employees from his inappropriate behaviour when they tried to hold him to account. He felt the rules shouldn’t apply to him and acted to save his own skin.”

According to an internal report conducted by an outside law firm, Mr Odey faced at least 46 allegations of inappropriate conduct during a 17-year period at his hedge fund.

Representatives for Mr Odey did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

During his appeal, the financier had argued that the FCA was under “political pressure” and had “sought a totemic case”, adding that the watchdog had a “pre-determined view of his fitness and propriety”.

The former hedge fund manager recently abandoned a libel suit against the Financial Times over its reporting on the sexual misconduct allegations.

Earlier this year, Mr Odey settled personal injury claims brought against him by five women for sexual assault. He strenuously denied any wrongdoing.

data.title: Trump’s childhood home sells for nearly $2m
data.description:
Donald Trump’s childhood home has sold for nearly $2m (£1.5m).

The US president’s father, Fred Trump, built the Tudor-style home in the Jamaica Estates neighbourhood of Queens in 1940. Mr Trump lived in the five-bedroom property until he was four.

The seller, real estate developer Tommy Lin, bought the house in Wareham Place for $835,000 in March 2025 after it had been sitting vacant and neglected for years.

It has now sold for $1.93m after undergoing a major renovation. The buyer’s identity has not been publicly disclosed.

According to the listing, the nearly 230 sq m home features “refined modern updates” including herringbone wood floors, a chef’s kitchen and “spa-like” bathrooms.

The Trump family has not owned the property for years, and it has changed hands several times since.

It sold for $2.14m in 2017, soon after Mr Trump entered the White House for his first term.

The house was then briefly available for rent on Airbnb for $800 a night, complete with a cardboard cutout of Mr Trump, copies of his book The Art of the Deal, and a framed magazine cover featuring the president.

When Mr Lin bought the house in 2025, it had fallen into disrepair after suffering damage from a burst pipe and mould. It had also become home to a colony of feral cats.

The developer spent $500,000 renovating the house. It was initially placed on the market for $2.3m before being relisted for $2m.

Joe Zhu, the listing agent for the property, said its connection to Mr Trump had been a major draw for prospective buyers.

“Quite a lot of people” were interested in buying the house because it was the president’s childhood home, he told the New York Post.

The listing did not shy away from the property’s history, describing it as a “true legacy property” and a “rare and extraordinary opportunity” to own Mr Trump’s childhood home.

Despite the Trump family not having lived at the property for decades, it has still occasionally attracted visitors.

After leaving the property, the Trump family moved into a 23-room brick mansion built directly behind their old back garden, and Mr Trump spent the rest of his childhood there.

Jamaica Estates has long been an affluent area of Queens. “Different parts of Queens were rough; this was an oasis,” Mr Trump said in a 2015 interview.

The president, now 80, earned his fortune in the real estate business – putting up his namesake Trump Tower in Manhattan and living there for decades – before moving into politics.

As president, he is overseeing his own residential overhaul, adding a ballroom to the White House, a controversial pet project of the president that has faced many obstacles, including several legal challenges.

data.title: Reform drums up business support at conference
data.description:
Large firms are flocking to Reform UK’s national conference as the party prepares to host its inaugural business day.

First Bus, BT, Vodafone, Google, Heathrow, JCB, Dubai Ports and TikTok are among the businesses sponsoring or running events at the three-day summit which starts on Thursday in Birmingham.

The party’s decision to host a business day forms part of a wider Reform UK strategy to replace the Conservatives as the main opposition party to Andy Burnham’s government by fighting Labour on economic grounds.

In recent weeks, the party has unveiled plans for the biggest welfare shake-up “in a generation” by scrapping key benefits to save £50bn a year, more than double what the Tories plan to save, as well as pledging a £30 rebate for taxpayers stuck on hold to His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs (HMRC).

To appeal to wealthy backers, they are also offering conference packages worth up to £3,000, which include a champagne breakfast with Nigel Farage, an opportunity to meet and network with senior Reform leaders and a three-course meal in the Platinum hospitality area.

‘Increased engagement’

The party has toned down its offerings from last year in an attempt to professionalise, scrapping offers of custom cocktail naming rights and the delivery of bottles of sparkling wine to business stands.

A Reform UK spokesman told The Telegraph: “Engagement from British business has increased significantly. Companies across the country recognise they need to understand Reform and what a future Reform government could mean for them.

“Businesses now realise that the possibility of a Reform government is very real and are acting accordingly.”

Until 2025, Reform had a relatively low attendance from big business compared with similar events organised by Labour and the Tories.

But the influx of big business to this year’s annual event signals that the corporate world is taking the possibility of a Reform government seriously, as the party continues to outperform rivals in voter intention polling.

Crypto sidelined

Reform, which topped polls for almost 16 consecutive months between March 2025 and July 2026 and won hundreds of councillors in May, is now in second place trailing the Labour Party following a so-called Burnham bounce.

Meanwhile, Mr Farage is also believed to be sidelining crypto companies in favour of mainstream corporates following a backlash over the Reform leader’s £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, the Bitcoin billionaire.

Crypto companies are not among the businesses sponsoring the 2026 conference, which last year included donations from crypto payments firm Zebec.

The party has also scrapped perks it had previously offered to crypto industry leaders, including free tickets and access to senior figures, according to City AM, in a notable departure from previous years.

Conferences and the sponsorship fees that come in from big businesses are one of the ways that political parties raise revenue for their campaigning efforts.

A Heathrow spokesman said the airport had “a long history of constructive engagement across the political spectrum”.

He said: “Like many businesses – from airlines to pubs and banks to supermarkets – it is common practice to sponsor events at party conferences to engage policymakers and ensure they better understand the needs of consumers and the economy.”

data.title: May Neptune curse the purveyors of false mackerel
data.description:
All things mackerel are heavenly in my view: from rippling cirrocumulus to freshly-caught fish on a monger’s slab, gleaming with the hues of the sea. As Vincent van Gogh wrote in a letter to his brother, “You don’t even know if it is green or violet, you can’t even say it’s blue”. Even the expression “holy mackerel” yields intense, salty satisfaction in a world of coarse expletives. If I were to die in summer, then I’d like my last meal to be grilled mackerel on salad, eaten minutes away from where it was caught. 

My menfolk tease me on my fetish. Our deep freeze is part-filled with mackerel fillets and I hoard tins of “emergency mackerel” in my larder and carry them in my tote bags for those vexing moments when you need a nutritious snack. (My big sister was amazed this summer to rifle through my rucksack and find a tin of M&S Hot Smoked Peppered Mackerel.) There are few things more delectable than tinned mackerel mashed with Hellmann’s mayonnaise and a handful of capers, layered on a rough oatcake. 

So, I’ve been rocked to learn that UK grocery giants Lidl, Aldi, Sainsbury’s and Tesco have quietly conspired with their supplier Prince’s to replace their tinned North Atlantic mackerel with the markedly inferior Chilean jack – placed on the same supermarket shelves under the same signage. Overfishing and plummeting fish stocks mean the northeast Atlantic variety can no longer be deemed “sustainable”, which has provided a handy excuse to substitute a cheaper variety. But Jack mackerel isn’t remotely the same beast. It’s from the Carangidae fish family, rather than Scombridae, and contains half as much omega-3 fatty acid as its rival and a third as much vitamin b12 (essential for red blood cell formation). Crucially, the traditional UK favourite is oilier, richer and tastier. Now I understand why I ended up throwing most of a tin away last week, thinking it was strangely devoid of succulence with a texture more like tuna. Even my Maine Coon disdained it.

Waitrose has shown itself to be an honourable player in the oily fish debacle, announcing its intention in February to phase out the sale of Atlantic mackerel while stocks are depleted. M&S and Asda still appear to be swimming in the North Atlantic swell, having checked my stack of tins last night. But may Neptune curse their competitors for trying to pull the scales over our eyes! A sleight of hand which is part of a wider, depressing trend for manufacturers to alter or downsize their products – what Which calls “skimpflation” – while hoping Mr & Mrs Muggins won’t notice. But if your taste buds are as sensitive to change as the princess who felt a pea underneath 20 feather mattresses, then you’ll be puce with rage at the audacity of the Great Taste Swindle.

I first flipped my lid on opening a packet of my beloved Montezuma’s 74 per cent cocoa chocolate buttons over a year ago and noting a smaller, duller, white-flecked and more brittle product (some writers run on caffeine, I run on cocoa). The melt-in-your mouth rich smoothness had vanished, vanilla extract had crept into the recipe and the weight was reduced. I wrote to their customer service department and left anguished reviews on TrustPilot under my wedded name MacKinnon, receiving stock responses that insisted consumers liked the new product.

The incident made me feel as hopeless as the monarch in A A Milne’s The King’s Breakfast who just wants “some butter for the Royal slice of bread”, only to be told, “many people nowadays like marmalade instead.” Butter lovers will never rest content with sharp, sugary marmalade and if your heart’s desire is oily mackerel, you won’t want some Chilean phoney. We all grasp the idea that there can be difficulties with supply chains and food must be produced sustainably. It’s the deception that hurts and the idea we won’t notice.

Why don’t our supermarket overlords turn necessity into virtue and promote British fish with the slogan, “Let them eat sardines!”

data.title: Britain spends £84bn on energy imports
data.description:
The UK spent £84bn on buying oil, gas and electricity from abroad last year, amid warnings that high taxes are killing jobs in the North Sea and risking energy security.

The figure is the highest since 2022, when Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine plunged Europe into the most severe energy crisis in decades.

A report by Offshore Energies UK (OEUK), which represents the oil, gas, hydrogen, carbon capture and offshore wind industries, also said imports accounted for more than 40pc of the country’s energy needs. It warned that this leaves families and firms more vulnerable to global disruption.

Energy prices have come under immense pressure from Donald Trump’s war with Iran. Last week, Labour delayed a decision on whether to approve the Jackdaw gas field and Rosebank oil project in the North Sea, which its backers say will boost energy security.

Gas prices in the UK have in recent days spiked to a four-year high, while oil prices surged as high as $108.50 a barrel.

The report warned that successive governments have undermined the UK’s domestic oil and gas sector, accelerating a decline in domestic production.

The UK will need 561 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas in the decade to 2035, it noted. The UK is expected to produce only 176bcm over this period. However, OEUK said this figure could be as high as 288bcm if the Government adopted “an investable fiscal regime and a pragmatic approach to licencing”.

If it does not, liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports could make up 46pc of supply by 2035, as opposed to only 6pc in a scenario where domestic production is prioritised.

The report warned: “LNG should be treated as a complement to domestic production, not a substitute. Future Norwegian piped imports also cannot be taken for granted.”

Norwegian officials have warned that supplies from the North Sea are in decline, threatening supplies to Britain, which relies on the Scandinavian country for around half of its gas.

LNG imports from the US rose by more than a third last year, increasing “exposure to global market volatility, geopolitical risk and higher lifecycle emissions”, the report said.

Three quarters of the LNG bought by the UK comes from the US, according to separate government figures.

The UK’s industrial energy consumption has meanwhile slumped to more than a 50-year low, amid industrial decline and greater power efficiency.

Enrique Cornejo, from OEUK, said: “It is concerning that we are importing more LNG, when we could produce half of our demand of gas for the coming years domestically with domestic resources. From the perspective of climate and emissions as well, LNG imports are more than three times more carbon-intensive compared to the average footprint of emissions in domestic [production]”.

The trade body urged Andy Burnham to scrap the Energy Profits Levy next year rather than in 2030, when the Government is planning to replace it with a 35pc tax on oil and gas sales.

Bringing in the oil and gas revenue levy three years early would help boost receipts by £14.9bn over the next decade, OEUK estimates.

The levy would have a less damaging effect on driving away investment, with £12.6bn of the boost to receipts coming from additional payroll taxes.

The report said: “The existing energy profits levy was introduced in response to a short-term price shock that has since ceased. The levy no longer reflects the market conditions and is constraining long-term investment in the UK continental shelf.”

data.title: Paying for speed: 5G ‘fast lanes’ risk steeper phone bills
data.description:
Speaking on the sidelines of Thruxton’s motor circuit in Hampshire on a soggy September afternoon, Max Taylor felt inspired.

“The UK needs to go faster,” the VodafoneThree boss said as he unveiled a new premium 5G service. “It’s what customers want, it’s what they’re asking us for – but it’s also what they’re going to need in the future.”

Vodafone’s new and improved 5G service will be a boon for Britons who have long struggled with scratchy calls and buffering videos.

This is just one frontier in a new era for the internet.

Alongside rivals Virgin Media O2 and BT-owned EE, Vodafone is calling for a watering down of crucial laws to help unleash faster 5G signals.

These reforms could open up a raft of new opportunities, the companies argue, from easing network congestion at concerts and sports events to allowing customers to prioritise urgent calls or online activities.

For consumers, however, access to these 5G fast lanes will probably come at a cost.

Slow and patchy mobile coverage is a reality of everyday life in Britain, which has download speeds so poor that they rank below countries including Kazakhstan and Cambodia.

Industry bosses and analysts point to a number of causes, including cumbersome planning laws and razor-thin margins that have stifled investment by network operators.

As 5G upgrades provide ever greater network capacity, there are now glimpses of improvement.

SuperMobile, Vodafone’s premium service, promises speeds up to four times faster than regular 5G.

EE has also launched its own fast-lane service, which offers speedier connections at crowded locations such as Wembley Stadium.

These innovations take advantage of 5G technology known as “slicing”, which allows different parts of a mobile network to be used for different purposes.

The changes come after Ofcom in 2023 revised its rules on net neutrality to clarify that mobile and broadband operators can offer premium services.

It was a modest revision of a decades-old principle dictating that all internet traffic and data must be treated equally.

Tearing through restrictions

Now, mobile network operators want to go further and tear up restrictions that prevent individual apps and services from being prioritised.

This could mean, for example, that a reveller trying to hail an Uber when leaving a busy venue would be prioritised over someone uploading videos of their night out to Instagram.

Equally, someone trying to connect to an electric-car charger in a multi-storey car park could be fast-tracked, while users could choose to prioritise an important video call over other activities.

For businesses, too, there are benefits. For example, a food stall operator could secure priority to process card payments or a ticketing company could secure extra bandwidth before an expected rush of sales.

BT, Virgin Media O2 and Vodafone are all lobbying ministers to allow these changes as part of the ongoing mobile market review.

“Outdated net neutrality rules mean that customers aren’t realising the full benefits of our investment,” says Jeanie York, VVMO2’s chief technology officer.

“Reforming these rules should be a priority for the Government, enabling operators to be more efficient in managing traffic and to use the full capabilities of the latest technology.”

A BT spokesman said: “The Mobile Market Review is an opportunity to modernise the regulatory and policy framework governing mobile networks, which was developed for a very different era of the internet almost 20 years ago.

“A more flexible approach to network management and innovation would help deliver better connectivity, support new technologies and encourage continued investment in world-class infrastructure for the UK.”

The industry argues that reform is all the more pressing as expanding AI use floods the internet with reams of additional data. After all, no one wants their connection to be slowed down by an army of AI agents and bots trawling the web.

Donald Trump has already torn up net neutrality rules in the US, providing a potential template for similar moves in the UK. Australia, Germany and Japan are among other countries that have taken a more permissive approach to the regulations.

Yet any attempt to water down net neutrality would prove controversial, not least in Silicon Valley.

Telecoms companies have been locked in a years-long tussle with tech giants over who should shoulder the network costs of data-heavy services such as Netflix and YouTube.

As it stands, network operators are blocked from charging these companies extra. But removing net neutrality requirements would open the door to extra fees – something the tech giants unsurprisingly resist.

Telecoms bosses deny that they want to inflict punitive fees on tech giants, insisting that any reform would instead be aimed at enabling optional premium services.

For many campaigners, however, net neutrality is a principle that goes well beyond any individual company and is instead a core tenet of the open web.

‘Commercial gatekeepers’

Critics warn that any move to discriminate between different types of data risks creating a “two-tier” internet where network operators control who sees what. This, they argue, could ultimately have implications for freedom of expression.

“Scrapping or relaxing these rules risks turning internet service providers into commercial gatekeepers,” says Alex Tofts, at Broadband Genie, a comparison site.

“Wealthy tech giants and enterprise clients could buy priority lanes, leaving everyday users and smaller independent businesses relegated to the digital slow lane.”

Perhaps most concerningly for consumers, these upgrades will come at a cost. Vodafone SuperMobile will cost contract customers an extra £3 a month, while EE’s upgraded service will be an extra £5.

In some ways, this seems reasonable. Most customers would accept the principle of paying a little bit more for a premium service, especially given UK mobile and broadband bills are significantly cheaper than in other countries such as the US.

“I think if we want better quality networks in more places, then there has to be a conversation about consumers needing to pay more,” says Matthew Howett, at Assembly Research.

“We’ve seen the effect of low prices in the lived experience of coverage for many people today.”

Howett draws a comparison with airline customers willing to fork out for a business class ticket. “At the moment, mobile operators are only allowing you to choose a higher baggage allowance,” he adds.

Yet some fear these new upgrades are the top of a slippery slope whereby consumers would be forced to shell out ever more to access the best service – or risk being left in the slow lane.

Mobile bosses insist that the reforms are about unlocking additional services for those willing to pay more, rather than charging extra to solve existing coverage problems. They argue that operators continue to invest in their networks to improve the service for all users.

Indeed, any extra revenue could be invested into the network to improve coverage for everyone, or even into cheaper tariffs for those who just want a basic service.

As mobile providers race to improve returns in a cut-throat market, however, some fear it is the customers who’ll end up footing the bill.

“Far more likely [is that] everyday customers may see their speeds throttled, effectively forcing them to upgrade to a more expensive tariff just to maintain the connection quality they previously enjoyed,” says Tofts.

data.title: JP Morgan boss meets Burnham and Healey amid fears of bank tax raid
data.description:
The boss of JP Morgan has met Andy Burnham and John Healey amid fears of a new windfall tax on banks.

Jamie Dimon, who has led the Wall Street lender for more than 20 years, met the Prime Minister and Chancellor in London on Wednesday after a phone call with the latter last month.

It comes just weeks before Mr Healey delivers his first Budget as Chancellor.

He is under pressure to find billions of pounds to repair the public finances after the fallout from the Iran war derailed the Government’s plans.

The American banker, who has met many chancellors during his period in charge of JP Morgan, was a strong supporter of Mr Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves.

“They are smart and dedicated and they are working with business and collaborating, which is the only way to make things work,” he said of the former chancellor and Sir Keir Starmer in an interview with The Sunday Times.

During Ms Reeves’s spell as chancellor, she resisted calls to raid lenders for more tax, calling financial services “the crown jewel in the UK economy” and instead encouraged regulators to relax rules in the City.

However, there are concerns that Mr Healey may raise levies on banks in his Budget on Oct 28.

Mr Burnham dropped into a meeting between Mr Dimon and Varun Chandra, the Prime Minister’s chief business adviser, according to the Financial Times.

Mr Dimon has previously warned Andy Burnham against the idea. The JP Morgan boss said in an interview earlier this year that there would be “adverse consequences” if Labour targeted lenders with fresh windfall taxes.

He said: “It would be one more negative on that bucket of things you got to think about.

“I always thought it was wrong. We’re a great citizen [in the UK]. We hire people there. We want to be bigger there. We train people there. We hire veterans there.”

The American banker added: “So if a government decides to do it, there’s nothing I can do, but it will over time cause decisions made that they may not like.”

There have been growing calls from unions and campaigners to raise taxes on banks.

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, has argued that Mr Burnham could raise £9bn in four years simply by reversing the previous Conservative government’s cut to the bank surcharge. The group has argued that this could be used to fund cuts to energy bills.

The Green Party also recently called for a 38pc windfall tax on banks to fund a tax cut for small businesses.

Jane Fraser, the boss of Citi, another Wall Street bank, has warned that any increase in taxes risks making the UK a prohibitively expensive place to do business.

She said during a visit to London last month that “money moves with its feet”, pointing out that “even Frankfurt and Paris are lower” when it comes to taxes for banks.

Mr Healey said this week that “doubling down” on “more growth generated in more places” will be a central priority of his first Budget.

He has refused to rule out raising taxes, but promised to “balance the books” and “control public spending”.

data.title: Global coal demand hits record high as Iran war cuts gas supplies
data.description:
Global coal consumption is set to hit a new record this year as war in the Middle East drives up global gas prices.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) said coal use would rise 1.2pc to a record 8.94 billion tonnes, after previously predicting that demand for the fossil fuel would decline.

The Paris-based agency said high gas prices and demand for air-conditioning, driven by the climate effect of the El Niño weather phenomenon, were pushing up coal consumption.

It linked the surge to the ongoing Iran war.

The agency said: “Although virtually no coal shipments pass through the Strait of Hormuz, the disruption has nonetheless affected coal markets by pushing up natural gas prices due to the plunge in liquefied natural gas shipments through the Strait.

“This has in turn encouraged more coal-fired generation in countries with gas-fired power fleets and spare coal capacity.”

The IEA predicted global demand for coal will “rise above previous expectations amid higher demand from import-dependent countries, such as Japan and Korea”, after global gas prices soared.

It added that this year’s so-called “Godzilla” El Niño weather pattern would lead to more coal demand from countries in Asia, such as India and Vietnam, as high temperatures lead to more demand for air-conditioning and lower hydropower output.

Coal use has been in long-term decline in Western economies as they switch to gas and renewables. However, usage has remained high in many developing economies and China, while Mr Trump has sought to encourage more coal production in the US.

A kilowatt-hour of power generated by burning coal typically releases a kilogram of CO2 – double that of gas. A typical UK household consumes 12,000 kilowatt-hours of energy a year.

The rise in coal use coincides with scientific reports that August was the world’s joint hottest month on record, with global temperatures at 1.65C above pre-industrial times.

Last month was the hottest August on record, with Western Europe experiencing its warmest ever summer, scientists from the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service said.

A run of heatwaves from May to August caused droughts in the UK, France, Hungary, Romania and Serbia, with major rivers, such as the Rhine and Danube, seeing exceptionally low flows.

Prof Friederike Otto, who specialises in climate science at Imperial College London, said: “You don’t need to be a climate scientist to see the evidence of climate change; you just need to look out of your window.

“Until we stop burning coal, oil and gas, these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming.”

The IEA said coal demand could increase again next year if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed.

data.title: Factories slash hiring ahead of Budget
data.description:
British manufacturers have cut back on hiring as they await greater certainty from John Healey’s Budget.

The balance of factories expecting to ramp up recruitment has dropped to just 3pc in the third quarter of this year, compared with 15pc in the previous three-month period.

While this indicates growth in hiring overall, the figures suggest it has slowed almost to a standstill.

As well as fears around the Budget, manufacturing trade body Make UK suggests factories are reluctant to recruit because of high taxes and inflated energy costs.

Manufacturing’s recruitment slowdown is compounded by a 6.2pc drop in the number of vacancies across the sector last quarter, according to the Office for National Statistics.

That is despite rising business confidence after manufacturers upgrading their forecast for UK output growth this year to 1.2pc, up 0.8pc.

But researchers said that although expectations appeared to be on the rise, this has not translated into job growth.

They said that factories are trying to do more with less as they battle growing cost pressures and red tape. Hiring has also been harmed by Labour’s Employment Rights Act, which has significantly strengthened workers’ rights.

Fhaheen Khan, a senior economist at Make UK, said: “The sharp slowdown in recruitment shows that high employment, energy and regulatory costs are forcing firms to think twice before taking on new people.”

Mr Khan added that the Budget will determine whether manufacturers will be able to “grow and invest”.

“Manufacturing makes up 10pc of the UK economy and could be vital to delivering the Prime Minister’s priorities,” he said.

Consumer confidence up

Separate findings from PwC also show an uptick in confidence among consumers, although economists warn that it could be short-lived, as rising food and energy prices put renewed pressure on household budgets.

The research shows consumer confidence reached its highest level in five years in August, with its sentiment index climbing from -13 in April to +1.

Almost two in five consumers described their finances as “healthy”, while fewer households expect to cut spending over the next three months.

But this growth in confidence risks being dampened by concerns about the cost of living, with 85pc of households citing this as one of their top worries, along with the state of the UK economy.

Sam Waller, the leader of industry for consumer markets at PwC UK, said: “As we head into autumn, the pressure on household finances will increase as energy and food prices rise.

“This will impact consumer facing businesses – along with wider macroeconomic headwinds that could spell higher interest rates and possible tax rises.

“Businesses should incentivise customers to start Christmas shopping now, and at the same, they must prepare themselves for a slowdown in consumer demand, look for ways to optimise operating costs, and to get their back-of-house in order.”

data.title: Try not to choke on the cost of your Sunday roast
data.description:
As the nights draw in and temperatures fall, families will soon be swapping burgers and barbecues for roast dinners.

But those cooking up a traditional Sunday meal are in for a shock – the price of a full roast has jumped almost 5pc in the last year, with warnings that worse could be on the way.

Prices are being driven up by all sorts of things: extreme weather has hit crop yields and pushed up the cost of what has been harvested; the size of Britain’s cattle and sheep herds is shrinking as farmers battle higher costs; and all agricultural businesses are facing higher bills for fuel, feed and other inputs, which are being passed on in the form of higher prices.

Labour’s “family farm tax” has hardly helped, with many agricultural businesses putting off investment as a result.

A roast dinner for the family with a 1kg joint of beef and all the trimmings now costs almost £27 to make, according to retail consultancy Assosia, up from £25.68 last year. A lamb roast now costs more than £23, compared with £21.96 last year.

The knock-on effect may be people enjoying a roast dinner less often, or cutting the size of their meals.

“People are buying less meat and they’re buying it less often,” says Sam Bagge, the general manager of the Walsingham Farm Shop on the north Norfolk coast.

Whole sirloin and topside joints are giving way to smaller cuts, he says. And prices that were changed only once a year are now being adjusted two or three times, he says, with offers and smaller packs used to keep products within customers’ budgets.

The cost of many ingredients in a roast is going up, but beef is the biggest culprit. Worldpanel by Numerator puts the average retail price at £12.11 a kilo, up 18pc in a year and more than 50pc in four years.

“The problem we’ve got at the moment is basically a reducing herd nationally year on year. Demand is roughly the same,” says Rob Woodhouse, a cattle farmer in Aberdeenshire.

Britain’s beef herd has been shrinking as farmers struggle with rising costs and poor returns. The size of the herd has fallen by about a third from its peak in the late 1990s.

Rising prices may prompt farmers to start expanding again, but it will take time. It can take three to five years for a farmer to see a return from increasing the size of their herd.

A shopping basket containing 1kg of beef and the usual potatoes, carrots, parsnips, cabbage and Brussels sprouts that accompany a roast now costs £26.87, up 4.6pc from last year, according to Assosia.

Surging prices for everyone

It’s not just home cooks who are feeling the pinch. At butcher HG Walter, Adam Heanen says chefs are putting less traditional cuts on the menu to keep roast beef affordable. Picanha, rump and chuck-eye are being used more often.

“Beef is still the firm favourite, but people are looking at different cuts,” he says.

“People still want that Sunday roast. It’s a special occasion and they want to push the boat out.”

It’s not just beef. Lamb is also becoming more expensive. Worldpanel records an average lamb price of £13.18 a kilo, up 4.6pc in a year and 19pc in five years. A full lamb roast with all the trimmings now costs £23.17, up 5.5pc in a year, according to Assosia.

Farmgate prices have risen by about 9pc, according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board.

Demand from Muslim consumers around Ramadan and Eid adds to seasonal pressure, while British lamb is also exported to continental Europe. At the same time, the number of breeding ewes in Britain has fallen to 14.7 million, the lowest number in living memory.

The outlook is less alarming for pork and chicken, which remain cheaper alternatives for households trying to keep the cost of a roast down.

But even here, prices are rising: Chicken now costs £5.17 a kilo on average, according to Worldpanel, up 1.7pc in a year, while pork is £6.39 a kilo, though this is up just 0.4pc.

So far, the vegetables in your roast have fared better. Potatoes are 1.3pc cheaper than a year ago, while parsnips, green cabbage and red cabbage have also fallen in price.

But the effects of this year’s drought may not be fully visible until later in the autumn and winter, when crops harvested now begin to emerge from storage.

Craig Elliot, who covers the UK potato market for commodity intelligence company Expana, says recent heatwaves have hit English crops particularly hard.

“Market players are suggesting that yields and quality could be significantly inhibited,” he says. “There is still a lot of uncertainty as we go through harvest.”

Scott Walker, the chief executive of GB Potatoes, says most supermarket potatoes are grown under contracts, meaning higher production costs do not immediately translate into higher prices for shoppers.

But customers will notice the poor harvest nonetheless.

“This year there will be smaller potatoes on the shelf, and I think that’s something the public is just going to have to accept, really,” he says.

This may be a sign of things to come. The National Audit Office said this month that disruption to Britain’s food system was becoming “more likely and potentially more severe”, citing extreme weather, cyberattacks and disease outbreaks.

Tom Bradshaw, the president of the National Farmers Union, said Britain had taken food availability for granted and warned against a repeat of the shortages seen after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Government says food security is a national security priority.

Nonetheless, prices will rise. The Food and Drink Federation forecasts that food inflation will peak at 6.4pc by July next year, with high price rises set to drag on for more than a year. Food already costs almost 40pc more than it did in 2020, on average.

There is some relief on the immediate outlook for meat. The price farmers receive for beef has fallen from more than £7 a kilo to about £6.12 over the past six months, which should eventually feed through to shoppers.

“I’d be staggered if the beef prices in the shops or the pork prices in the shops are higher than they are now,” says David Swales, of the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board.

But Woodhouse is sceptical.

“I think the reducing herd is going to be the biggest cause of price increases going forward, rather than the drought,” he says.

For those hoping for a return to the affordable roast dinner of yesteryear, this will be difficult to swallow.

data.title: How a ‘Frankenstein’ open-plan house was transformed into a cosy, colourful home
data.description:
“Frankenstein” is the word the owners, a professional couple with three children, use to describe the previous incarnation of this 1930s terrace, which they bought on their return to north London after living in Amsterdam for work.

It’s a little unkind. The house has good bones, generous rooms and good proportions. But at some point, it had been given the full treatment – a large rear extension, a loft conversion and a fashionable open-plan layout with lots of hard finishes – making it cavernous and unwelcoming.

“The owners chose it for the location and because they could see its potential. But it didn’t work for how they lived,” explains interior designer Carina Raymond, founder of London-based Studio Raymond, who was tasked with the redesign. “They wanted areas that felt cosy and private, and a separate space for the children to use, especially when they had friends over.”

Her solution included adding a partition wall to the kitchen and dining area to make both sections more intimate and allow extra seating for guests when food is being prepared, blocking off the doors between the sitting room and games room to create a family room and formal reception room; and replacing the half-height partition wall dividing the games room from the kitchen-dining space with a set of arches, which create privacy and a natural flow into the dining room.

Upstairs comprised four bedrooms and one bathroom. Here, Raymond stole space from one of the bedrooms to make a large main bedroom and repurposed one of the smaller bedrooms as an en suite. Conversely, at the top of the house, the large bedroom was divided into two, creating a study and guest room, and the en suite was turned into a standalone bathroom.

Once the layout had been reconfigured, it was time to decorate. The owners’ home in Amsterdam, as well as their previous London home, had a neutral, Scandinavian-inspired design, and they were ready for a change. “They wanted to embrace colour, fun and pattern, and to tap into English suppliers, but weren’t sure how to achieve exactly the look they wanted.”

Starting with a couple of images the owners had included in the brief, as well as several wallpapers they liked, Raymond built up complex, layered schemes, using suppliers including Cole & Son, Porta Romana, Matilda Goad, and GP&J Baker to create something bold, but liveable, with a distinctly English sensibility.

Entrance

The roomy entrance was made more practical with storage for coats, bags, and shoes, and a built-in bench. Walls have been colour-drenched in Tawny by Edward Bulmer, a pleasing foil to woodwork in Green Smoke by Farrow & Ball. “I’ve used this colour on the woodwork all the way up the house to create a link between downstairs and upstairs,” says Raymond.

The owners didn’t want a traditional black-and-white floor, so she opted for a softer chequer-board effect with marble tiles in cream and white. The space is further softened by textured paper by Phillip Jeffries inset into the cupboard doors and a silk pendant light by Gong, which gives off a warm, diffused light.

Family room

For the family room, the owners wanted something moody and liked the idea of a denim effect on the walls. In answer, Raymond used a silk wallpaper from Phillip Jeffries, which has similar variations to denim, and Wine Dark, a rich blue by Farrow & Ball on the ceiling, cornices, fireplace, and joinery. To this, she has added accents of primary colours inspired by the owners’ existing artworks that brighten the space and add a sense of fun.

The owners didn’t have many pieces of furniture to reuse, but a handful appear in this room, including the graphic green and black rug, the L-shaped sofa, which Raymond updated with scatter cushions in Wriggle Room and Potato Print by GP&J Baker; and the ottoman, which has been reupholstered in Runaway, also by GP&J Baker.

Reception room

“This spicy shade of yellow aptly called Cinnamon by Edward Bulmer is a sunny hug – perfect for a space that doesn’t get direct sunlight,” notes Raymond.

A pair of striking, large-scale bespoke armchairs covered in Sophie, a terracotta stripe by Manuel Canovas, has a similar enlivening effect, which Raymond has deftly balanced with a big sofa in neutral weave and a simple sisal rug by Peter Page.

A fireplace surround in Calacatta Viola marble, a chandelier by Soho Home, and a vintage travertine coffee table, which picks up the colour of the walls, add notes of glamour.

Kitchen and dining room

An extendable walnut dining table by Alfred Newall makes a handsome centrepiece for the dining room. It is combined with the Molina chairs from Soho Home in a mix of fabrics. “There are quite a few; I didn’t want it to feel samey.”

The kitchen had a practical layout and was in fine condition, so the cabinets were simply repainted and given new ironmongery. To seat more at the island, the top was replaced with a piece of Rosso Orobico marble with a large overhang.

Raymond also found space for a generous walk-in pantry, which greatly increases the kitchen’s storage capacity, and is painted in Brinjal, a lush shade of aubergine, by Farrow & Ball.

Main bedroom and en suite

The main bedroom was designed around the owners’ existing bed, and has panelling in the same style as the dining and reception rooms. This adds architectural interest and lends the house a sense of cohesion.

Raymond has given it a calm, whimsical atmosphere by painting the walls in Aerial Tint, a light powdery blue by Edward Bulmer, papering the ceiling in a cloudscape by Schumacher, and adding a silk pendant light by Gong with a cloud-like shape.

In contrast, the large ensuite bathroom is dramatic and opulent, thanks to the strong veining of the Calacatta Arabescato tiles.

Children’s bedroom and bathroom

Raymond was mindful to give the children’s rooms designs they could grow into. For the girls, she has chosen a neutral, textured wallcovering by Schumacher and a bobbin trim; twin beds upholstered in a Backdrop by GP&J Baker, and a row of smart, built-in cupboards.

The owners’ son wanted a forest theme for his room, so she built the scheme around the Raphael wallpaper in blue by Sandberg. She has rationalised this long, thin space by devoting one third to built-in cupboards and a desk painted in Hague Blue by Farrow & Ball.

In the shared bathroom, neutral finishes dominate: Zellica Antique White wall tiles from Topps Tiles and Pearl floor tiles by Bert and May are all lifted by a zingy yellow vanity unit and wall lights by Pooky with colourful shades.
