data.title: I travelled the ‘border’ between North and South. Here’s what I learnt
data.description:
A sign by the estuary warns of danger, but it’s hard to see much to be afraid of here apart from the nettles and a fairly ominous sky. Under the Severn Bridge, on a spit of land on the river’s west side, it seems peaceful enough. Traffic roars overhead, but you can’t see the cars from below. There’s birdsong and the smell of wet foliage, glimmering water fringed by sodden sand and then cracked earth. It doesn’t feel like a border, but I’m standing at the far western end of England’s North-South divide.

There is, of course, no official line across England’s midriff. No razor-wire fences or passport checks mark where the South ends and the North begins. But nor is the boundary a figment of our imagination. We’ve heard enough jokes about the Watford Gap to know that Southerners see the North – the people, the places, the culture – as somehow different. And we Northerners, admittedly, can be bloody-minded about our Northern identity.

But how entrenched does the North-South divide remain today, after years of political talk of levelling up, Northern powerhouses and ill-fated high-speed rail connections? How much does our geography still shape how we see those from elsewhere in the country? And where, actually, does the notional dividing line start and end?

Apparently, not where you might expect. Recent YouGov data from almost 46,000 adults in England revealed that many people along the borders of the areas classified as North, South and Midlands don’t place themselves in the same regions government maps would suggest. Feelings of “Northernness” extended south of the regional borders, the pollsters found, while in the parts of East Anglia that supposedly sit in the South, people don’t all feel Southern. In short, like many types of identity, it’s complicated.

With that in mind, I have set out to travel along an unofficial boundary line between the North and South of England – one commonly used in academic research – to interrogate these feelings and explore what the divide means today. My editor has suggested I walk the entire 340 miles from Beachley Point on the Severn estuary to the Wash, between Lincolnshire and Norfolk, possibly in one go. I have counter-suggested the use of a motor vehicle.

The journey is a personal one. Having grown up in Leeds, my Northern identity is one I have insisted on throughout my adult life (which I’ve spent mostly in the South). When I started writing my debut crime thriller novel, The House on Otley Road, I knew it had to be set in West Yorkshire. Home.

The tug of the North has never left me, and I spend much of my time on the East Coast Main Line, travelling to and from where I spent my youth. But I’m surprised to find that it supposedly begins more or less where I’m standing by the Severn. The first (and only) person I encounter on the footpath here is Justin Charnock, 37. He identifies as Southern (this is fair – he comes from near Bristol) and thinks “people in the North are a lot nicer than people in the South” (also fair). “More welcoming,” he says.

It’s a commonly held perception, mentioned frequently by those I meet on my journey – almost all of whom have strong ideas about how Northerners differ from Southerners.

Charnock thinks being Southern traditionally means being “wealthier; a lot more aloof; snobby; much less hospitable, welcoming, friendly or helpful”. Working in the South West (he won’t divulge his job), he never gets tipped and “often people are a bit snooty”.

‘It’s become very middle class here’

Behind the popular images of Northerners lie some dispiriting numbers. The North East remains the region with the lowest healthy life expectancy at birth (HLE), at 57 years, according to the most recent figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS). It has had the lowest HLE in every period since the ONS began measuring it. The South East remains the region with the highest HLE (63 years for men, 64.3 years for women).

A similar disparity can be seen in economic activity. In 2023, London had the highest gross domestic product per capita, at £69,077, while the North East had the lowest, at £28,583. It is worth noting, though, that the poverty rate is higher in London (26 per cent) than anywhere else in the country, according to figures from the charity Joseph Rowntree Foundation.

Meanwhile, perceptions of Northerners and Southerners that seem to stem from our economic histories – the North as industrial, the South as the country’s financial engine – have stubbornly persisted.

The first stop on my journey is Brockweir, a scenic Gloucestershire village on the river Wye. Old stone houses are painted in creamy yellow, pale blue and white, while green hills rise behind them. All the villagers seem to know each other. They all have dogs, and their dogs know each other too. The community owns its pub, the 16th-century Brockweir Inn.

“We tried to sell our bodies [to raise the money for it], but we’re all too old,” says Carol Knight, 76. (I think she’s joking.)

Her family has lived here for centuries. “It’s become very middle class,” says the suntanned, denim-dungaree-clad former English teacher, while clutching a bunch of Whitsuntide boss flowers and the leads of her two labradors. “Property prices have skyrocketed.”

Does this mean Brockweir must be Southern? House prices are, after all, a stark divider between North and South. Prices may be rising more steeply in the North at present, but the gap remains vast, even after removing London from the equation: in March 2026, the average house price across the South East and South West was £340,000, compared with £188,500 across the North East and North West.

‘We need more Northern leaders’

I travel onwards, trying to keep close to the Wye, down winding lanes bordered by verdant hedgerows and cow parsley. I stop at Upper Redbrook, where I can’t find a pub, or a shop, or a human, then Staunton, where the 18th-century pub isn’t open yet (it’s still too early). Traffic rattles through the village of silent modern houses.

In the Herefordshire village of Lea, I encounter a friendly pair of Scousers who decamped here long ago. Mike Tyson, a 46-year-old roofer and carpenter (“Yes, it’s my real name,” he says, for probably the millionth time), talks of his daughter’s “Northern attitude”.

What is it? “Friendlier, more easy-come, easy-go. ‘Chippy’ is the right phrase.”

The men are not the only ones to claim Northerners have a different (better?) sense of humour. But there’s uncertainty about whether we’re in the North or the South here – the consensus seems to be the middle – but Tyson believes there’s more money to be made down here than up in Liverpool.

Tied up with the question of economic activity and affluence is that of political power. Devolution to England’s cities and regions has given some control to communities far from Westminster. Whether it has helped those communities feel less overlooked is uncertain. Phil Henesey, 71, who is drinking in a beer garden with Tyson in the late-afternoon sunshine, says the North still feels farther (figuratively) from Westminster decision making.

“That’s why we need more Northern leaders,” he says.

He is speaking not long before the enthroning of a Northern leader in Downing Street. Andy Burnham, the Liverpool-born former Mayor of Greater Manchester, has made much of his links to, and concern for, the North of England. The new PM has created a No 10 North. In doing so, he has set himself up to be judged on how successfully he makes Northerners feel more connected to the centre of power. Also on how he does this without alienating the South.

‘There’s more chivalry in the North’

It’s raining when I reach Ledbury, the sky a grey-white sheet. The Tudor buildings are picture-perfect and well preserved. “It’s very much Middle England,” says a shopkeeper on the high street who doesn’t want to be named. “Did you ever see Keeping up Appearances? It’s full of Hyacinth Buckets [here].”

He identifies as a Southerner. “When you go up North, it’s dark,” he says. “It’s a funny old thing, that divide.”

Declan Butler, a 68-year-old Irishman who moved to Britain in the 1970s and now runs a gift shop down the road, thinks Ledbury is “probably more Southern”, judging by its disposable income.

“I had a couple in here from North Yorkshire at the weekend and they spoke to me as if we were old friends, whereas people from the South East are much more reserved,” he says. “If I was to choose a Southerner or a Northerner to be friends with, I’d choose a Northerner, because they’re friendlier. They’re probably harder workers. They’re grafters.”

He concedes that Cockneys and people from Essex can be friendly, too. Has he been to the North much? “I’ve been to Birmingham,” he offers.

Crossing into Worcestershire, I see the grey-blue shadow of the hills rise up ahead. I pass an old roadside chapel and an abandoned filling station, and arrive at Bredon, where the local Spar sells cider on tap.

“I thought the North started at Crewe,” muses Steve Fowler, an ex-Army man, inside the still-quiet Royal Oak pub, where there’s horse racing on the TV. He’s surprised to hear that by some definitions he is in the North right now. A Southerner by birth (Surrey), he awards the North another point for humour. “The funniest comedians are Northerners,” he says.

“I think [people] are more materialistic in the South,” says David Gray, a semi-retired gardener from Scotland. “There’s a lot more chivalry in the North.”

“It’s all about survival in the North,” chips in Paul Sefton, a retired butcher. He came here from North Wales 30 years ago “purely because someone said to me my kids would never get a proper job up North”.

‘The Cotswolds is becoming the Home Counties’

The North-South divide has been with us for a long time, chronicled and perpetuated by our art and culture. Elizabeth Gaskell’s North and South (published 1855) contrasts England’s tranquil, idyllic South with a grimy industrial North plagued by poverty and suffering. Almost 150 years later, David Peace evoked a dark and lawless North in his fictional Red Riding quartet. There was always something harder and edgier about the most famous Northern bands than their Southern counterparts. Contrast the Beatles with the Kinks, Oasis with Blur.

Yet in today’s hyperconnected society, how long can such differences last?

“It’s flattened out quite a bit by sheer mobility,” says Steve Fowler. And, he says, by exposure to the internet. “You would have to go very deep into the countryside, to very isolated communities, to find residual differences.”

In the Plough Inn in Stretton-on-Fosse, Warwickshire, Gordon Everett, 59, says, with both sadness and pride, “This is one of the last old-fashioned drinking pubs.” Local accents are waning a lot, he says, touching on the most overt marker of Northern or Southern identity. When he was a boy, you could tell the difference in accents between people from two local villages that lay just three miles apart. “Now, everyone’s got this flat English accent.”

Non-locals, he says, have come to the area and changed it. “The Cotswolds is becoming the Home Counties.”

Still, tracing this line across the country is a lesson in the extent to which our villages and small towns either cling to their past or else are haunted by it. Between Bredon and Stretton-on-Fosse, I pass houses with names such as the Old Bakehouse, the Old Stoves. A croquet club and a country clothing store. Less picturesque: a dead badger on the A44.

In Brackley, Northamptonshire, there’s a similar nostalgia in evidence. On the high street, there’s the Old Bakery and the Old Hall Bookshop. The sign for Brackley Community Shops is painted in old-fashioned fairground colours. One of these shops offers tattoos, but still.

In the Courtyard Shops farther along, I’m reminded of one of those mock-Victorian streets you find in museums, except there’s a vape shop here. Browsers are welcome, says a sticker in the window, and they’re also on CCTV.

A 75-year-old woman I meet in the town, when I ask what Northerners are like, suggests they’re either industrious farmers or else they work in “industrial places”. I don’t have the heart to tell her that no one I know in West Yorkshire does any such thing.

Did you know Brackley is in fact north of the North-South divide, I ask Anne Mellor, a volunteer in a local charity shop? “No,” she says, “we thought we were in the middle, surrounded by HS2.”

Depending on where you are in the North, transport links can be a sore point – and another marker of difference from the South. Burnham might be proud of his re-regulated Bee Network buses in Manchester, but raise the subject of the still-non-existent tram service in Leeds and that fabled Northern grit might give way to heavy sighs of Northern frustration.

In the North East, poor transport links were said last year to put more than 30 per cent of the region at risk of poverty. In 2022, lack of transport connectivity was found by the Centre for Cities to cost the North £16bn a year in productivity losses. Against this backdrop, HS2 has become a punchline, not an answer.

‘They’re parochial and territorial’

I’m travelling to Silverstone, Northamptonshire, which is famous for a different sort of transport. Pictures of motor-racing heroes adorn the walls of the village pub, the White Horse. I pass through a familiar landscape of roundabouts and roadworks before arriving. A poster on the village noticeboard invites me to become the best version of myself. (I decline.)

Gary Baird, 38, who runs the pub, thinks the North is more working class, while the South attracts more tourism. No one, he argues, goes to Hull on holiday.

Onwards to Rushden, Northants, a “historic boot and shoe town”, passing en route an American diner, a Starbucks, a Travelodge, a McDonald’s, a Toby Carvery and a new-build housing estate. I could be anywhere now. I don’t know whether I’m North or South, my senses are scrambled, or numbed by the dreary uniformity of our in-between spaces.

But in Rushden, for the first time, I feel I could be in the North. Behind the bar in the town’s Working Men’s Club, 30-year-old Tomethia Bartley confirms, “They’re Northerners here.” (She’s not – she’s from London.) “They’re all in a community together. Everyone knows everyone.”

She’s wearing a T-shirt saying, “Don’t like me? F--- off. Problem solved.” I don’t know how Northern or Southern this sentiment is.

Howard, 67, a former helicopter pilot enjoying a pint in the club with his partner, Lynette Keirnan, says: “I was married to a woman from Lancashire. She was bloody weird, actually. They seem to see things differently up there. They’re very parochial and territorial.

“They eat food like barm cakes [a bread roll from the North West] and black peas,” he adds. “They feel disenfranchised, I think.”

But out on the high street, it doesn’t feel so different here from many post-industrial towns further North, with grand old Victorian buildings and the sense of better days being behind it. There’s a kebab shop and an amusement arcade now. A nail bar, a Poundstretcher and, curiously, a large reptile specialist called House of Venom.

Deeply ingrained perceptions

The land flattens out as I enter Lincolnshire, stopping briefly in Market Deeping for a scalding portion of battered fish. “Sunny days are here at last,” it says on a small blackboard inside the Market Gate Deli. Outside, a fine rain falls. An unseasonable chill hangs in the early June air.

My odyssey ends in Norfolk, where I meet arable farmer Richard Ward, 55. “Where am I?” I ask.

“You’re probably North more than anything, because that’s the North Sea,” he says, pointing to the horizon, where I can’t see anything but farmland. A few years ago, a bomb squad came to remove a load of Second World War ordnance found in the fields. “It was quite a hairy experience,” says Ward.

Do people fish out there? I ask, pointing vaguely to where the sea should be. No, he says. “It’s dead vegetation and horrible black, boggy clay soil.”

I finish my journey not far from this, by a soggy field overlooking some marshland. The sun has finally emerged. Some desultory wasps buzz above the glistening wet grass. A crow caws, a cockerel crows and my feet are becoming very wet.

The conversations I’ve had along my journey have shown that, despite our increasingly homogenised culture, perceptions of differences between Northerners and Southerners remain deeply ingrained. Perhaps we will always retain these in some form.

As Richard Collett writes in his book Along the Borders, “We carve landscapes apart to define our very sense of self and identity.”

I recognise this impulse. And I’m not going to claim it’s all grim down South, but I’ll always be Northern and proud.

The House on Otley Road by Rosa Silverman (£16.99, HQ/HarperCollins) is out now.

data.title: Foreign investors sour on Britain after Labour tax raids
data.description:
Overseas investment in Britain has dropped sharply in the wake of Labour’s tax raids.

Foreign direct investment (FDI) sank by £14bn, or 21pc, to £54bn last year, according to new figures from the City of London Corporation. Overseas investors cut the number of large projects they backed across Britain.

Sovereign wealth funds and global public pension funds cut investment in the UK by £3bn to £19bn in 2025. The UK’s share of global sovereign investment declined from 13pc to 9pc last year, even as overall investment activity grew globally.

Chris Hayward, the policy chairman for the City of London Corporation, warned: “The UK is losing ground to international competitors.

“Some of this is cyclical, but we must confront adverse trends early: strengthening the UK’s offer to global investors and ensuring that domestic capital is channelled more effectively into productive UK assets.”

The corporation noted that sovereign cash was behind strategic assets including Heathrow, Gatwick, National Grid and Rolls-Royce’s small modular reactor programme.

Mr Hayward added that growing the UK economy depended on “investment across our nations and regions”, with overseas money an important part of that.

Business targeted

The drop in FDI follows a series of tax raids by the Government. A crackdown on non-doms alongside changes to inheritance tax have prompted entrepreneurs to warn that Britain is becoming unwelcoming to wealthy people.

Figures from HMRC showed that the number of non-doms shrank by 1,200 in the financial year ending April 2025.

There are concerns that wealthy entrepreneurs will be first in the firing line for a fresh tax raid under John Healey’s maiden Budget on Oct 28.

Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, also targeted businesses with an increase in employer National Insurance contributions. At the same time, investors have complained that Britain’s sclerotic planning system and high energy costs have made it unattractive.

OpenAI abandoned plans to construct a data centre in the North East earlier this year, citing energy costs.

In other cases, politicians have intervened. Ministers blocked China’s Ming Yang from establishing a wind turbine factory in Scotland on national security grounds in March. Ming Yang insisted it posed no threat.

While FDI fell, total investment across the UK rose 5pc to £4.1tn last year because of an increase in domestic activity.

The Treasury was contacted for comment.

data.title: FTSE aerospace supplier sold to US bidder for £1.9bn
data.description:
A 103-year-old UK aerospace supplier is poised to leave the London stock market after being sold to a US private equity firm.

Bodycote, which is one of the world’s leading metallurgy companies, is to be taken over by New York’s Veritas Capital for £1.85bn.

It will see the Macclesfield company enter private hands for the first time in more than half a century, following its initial stock market listing in 1972.

Bodycote’s takeover is one of a trio of deals announced on Tuesday that will reignite concerns about the ailing health of the London stock market.

Gamma Communications, a FTSE 250 telecoms company, separately agreed a £1.1bn sale to Epris, a London private equity firm. Capricorn Energy, a Scottish oil-and-gas company, struck a deal to sell itself to Norway’s oldest oil company, DNO, for £292m.

Bodycote is the world’s biggest provider of specialist metallurgical treatments, spanning a global network of around 135 workshops.

The FTSE 250 company was started as a textiles manufacturer in Leicestershire in 1923 before moving into the metallurgy industry in the 1970s.

The metals it makes are used in everything from Rolls-Royce’s aerospace engines to specialist drills for undersea mines. It has around 4,000 employees.

The takeover will see Bodycote’s shareholders paid 940p per share, marking a 44pc premium on its closing price on July 7, the day before Veritas submitted its initial offer.

James Dimitri, from Veritas, said: “Bodycote has established itself as a global leader in providing essential technologies for performance metallurgy across a range of mission-critical end markets.”

Veritas is an American private equity firm with around $42bn (£36bn) worth of investments.

Since its launch, Veritas has made more than 145 acquisitions of mostly British and American businesses, including Scottish energy consultancy Wood Mackenzie in 2023.

London’s shrinking stock market

The takeover is the latest in a series of acquisitions that have seen some of Britain’s biggest companies pulled off the London Stock Exchange.

Capricorn Energy, which also announced a deal to go private on Tuesday, owns stakes in four oil and gas fields in the Egyptian desert, and is exploring more sites in the area.

DNO, which was started in 1971, is listed on the Oslo Stock Exchange and has oil sites in the Middle East, West Africa and the North Sea.

Berkshire-based Gamma sells phone and internet services to businesses across Western Europe, including the University of Derby and the AA.

Low valuations have made London-listed companies attractive to international buyers. It has fuelled an exodus from the London Stock Exchange, with the number of listed companies falling from 2,365 a decade ago to around 1,500 today.

Most recently, Tate & Lyle was taken over by US rival Ingredion in a £2.7bn deal in June that ended its 90-year stint on London’s main market.

Wise cancelled its listing on the London Stock Exchange in May after shifting its primary listing to New York. Flutter Entertainment, which owns Betfair and Paddy Power, shifted its own listing from London to New York in 2024.

data.title: Railways at risk as weeks of record-breaking heat damages soil
data.description:
Around 20 per cent of England’s railways are vulnerable to derailment because of this year’s record-breaking heat, experts have warned.

About a fifth of railways in the country are built on clay soil, which can become very hard when dry, causing them to shrink and crack – and for anything built on top of them to move or subside.

Roughly 1,800 miles of rails lie on clay ground in areas classed as having a high or very high risk of drought, nature investment fund Rebalance Earth has said.

Rebalance Earth shared its findings after two train derailments took place less than 24 hours apart. Last week, a service came off the tracks just outside Lewes, East Sussex, injuring 30 people. A day later, another train derailed in Wickford, Essex.

Both incidents are under investigation by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB), with experts looking into the effect of hot and dry weather on the railways.

Investigators are examining whether the East Sussex accident could have been caused by conditions making the ground shift, causing the rails above to buckle.

A picture released by the RAIB shows a visible buckle or kink in the rails that was visible 20 minutes before the derailment.

Prof Neil Entwhistle, of Rebalance Earth, warned that clay soils – including the ground under the tracks in Lewes – are especially vulnerable to shifting when they dry out after prolonged hot and dry conditions.

“The RAIB’s initial report notes that the railway at Lewes is built on clay and alluvium that are sensitive to changes in water content, with evidence that some ground movement had already occurred,” he said.

“Investigators also identified a track geometry irregularity on the approach to the derailment, meaning the rails had shifted or become uneven, with ground movement being one potential cause,” he added.

The British Geological Survey has described the clay shrink–swell cycle as “the most damaging geohazard in Britain today”, warning that it can cause subsidence in houses as well as tens of millions of pounds in insurance claims.

Prof Entwhistle and Gabrielle Edghill, a geospatial analyst, graded each area of clay across the country for its drought risk, assigning them ratings between “very low” and “very high”. They then cross-referenced this model with the locations of all 10,000 miles of railway lines in Great Britain.

Ms Edghill said: “Uneven shrinkage beneath a railway can alter the position and level of the track, potentially creating an irregularity that requires speed restrictions, tamping or other intervention.”

There are a number of places in Britain where clay is the dominant type of ground. Most notably, this includes London, which is where the name of the colour “London Clay” originates.

Other types of clay include Wealden, Wadhurst, Oxford and Mercia Mudstone and there are various railway lines laid on top of those soils across southern England. However, not every railway line laid in a clay area is necessarily built on a clay embankment.

The Victorian engineers responsible for building the railways favoured these flat, low-lying grounds because it kept construction costs down.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, reportedly asked rail bosses whether anything “needed to be done across the network as a whole” after the incident in Wickford.

As reported by Rail magazine, Lord Hendy, a rail minister, said: “The Secretary of State asked on Friday afternoon [Aug 14] the most senior people in Network Rail, the operator, and the ORR [Office of Rail and Road] whether or not there was anything as a consequence of having two instances in a very short space of time that needed to be done across the network as a whole.”

Greater Thameslink Railway, which operates Southern-branded trains across the south of England, said earlier this week that the line between Lewes and Haywards Heath would not reopen until Sept 1.

A Network Rail spokesman said: “We have a range of techniques for managing drying clay around the railway.

“These include using technology to monitor our tracks and trackbed, maintaining the lineside to minimise water-hungry trees, and most importantly, preparing for summer with a programme of targeted track maintenance.

“With that work and the £2.6bn we are investing in climate resilience, our railway will be safe and reliable for years to come.”

data.title: Pubgoers to use digital ID to buy drinks
data.description:
Pubgoers will be able to use digital ID on their phones to prove they are more than 18 when buying alcohol under new rules.

Pubs, supermarkets and other retailers will be able to accept digital age checks at the till or bar starting on Tuesday. The digital ID will be linked to a physical ID such as a passport.

The Telegraph understands several major retailers and pub groups are interested in adopting the technology. Some smaller operators will be able to access the ID-checking services free.

The Government has likened the rollout to the spread of contactless payments, with adoption expected to build as more businesses begin accepting digital ID.

Digital ID companies have grown rapidly as governments and technology companies have tightened online age checks. One of the biggest players in the market said it now processes around one million a day.

The surge has been driven in part by the Online Safety Act 2023, which has required pornography sites to introduce strict age checks using facial age estimation and photo-ID checks since last year.

But the system being opened up for alcohol will require more rigorous verification measures.

Customers will have to prove their identity using a genuine document before they can create a digital ID. Those using a passport can scan the chip inside the document with their phone to verify it is genuine.

At the bar, they scan their face to unlock a QR code that expires after about 30 seconds, making it harder to pass a digital ID to someone else.

The launch of widespread digital checks for alcohol purchases comes after trials of the technology in supermarkets.

The change is separate from Sir Keir Starmer’s plans for a national digital ID, which were abandoned by Andy Burnham this year after opposition over privacy and civil liberties.

Stephanie Peacock, the digital government minister, said: “You do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information such as your name or address just to prove your age.”

Martin Ashley, the landlord of the Blue Posts on Berwick Street, Soho, which was one of the first pubs to embrace the technology, said it could help tackle increasingly sophisticated fake IDs.

He said: “We spend a lot of money on making sure there are no underage drinkers, and also on crime prevention, because we’re in a hotspot – the centre of London – and there’s a lot of activity that goes on.

“I think that is the future, as long as it doesn’t creep into everyday life.”

Businesses will not be forced to accept digital ID, and customers can keep using physical documents.

The rules apply to licensed businesses across England and Wales.

data.title: Volkswagen to slash up to 50,000 jobs
data.description:
Volkswagen’s shares have surged after the German giant confirmed plans to cut 50,000 jobs as it battles competition from China.

The carmaker’s Frankfurt-listed shares jumped by more than 8pc on Friday after it unveiled the sweeping job cuts, which are the biggest in Volkswagen’s 89-year history.

Volkswagen said on Thursday it would cut tens of thousands more roles as it faces fierce competition from Chinese rivals that are flooding into Europe.

The German carmaker said that the restructuring would be in addition to 50,000 reductions that it has already made since 2024 and could lead to plant closures.

It is racing to cut costs as it grapples with fierce competition from Chinese rivals such as BYD and slowing demand in Europe. It has also struggled under US tariffs and Volkswagen vehicle sales fell by 8.4pc in the first half of the year, while its operating profit dropped by 11.6pc.

News of the restructuring plans emerged earlier this year, but had yet to be approved by Volkswagen’s supervisory board, which represents the labour force and shareholders.

The carmaker said its European capacity “currently exceeds demand by more than 500,000 units”. The new plan will pave the way for Volkswagen to slim its vehicle line-up by as much as 50pc by 2035.

“Given intensifying global competition, shifting demand and technological change in the automotive industry, a consistent alignment of workforce capacity with economic reality is essential,” the company said in a statement.

Last September, Porsche, which is owned by Volkswagen, blamed a decision to delay the launch of its new electric SUV in September on weak demand for electric cars as it warned of a €5.1bn (£4.4bn) hit to profits.

Volkswagen added that it could not guarantee that a number of its plants would be used from 2030 onwards. It said it was considering alternative uses for the four affected factories. Some could potentially be converted into use by Germany’s defence industry.

Oliver Blume, the Volkswagen chief executive, said last month that the company was in talks with defence companies to use its site in Osnabrück.

The new cuts represent about 8pc of the company’s global workforce of roughly 650,000 across brands such as Škoda, Seat, Porsche and Lamborghini.

It comes after lengthy talks between the company, its unions and Lower Saxony, the German state where the company is headquartered. The state is also a large minority shareholder in Volkswagen.

Mr Blume has previously said that Volkswagen needed to rein in costs, which were roughly 30pc higher than its competitors. The company said it was seeking to lift its margin to 9pc by 2030, up from just 3.8pc in the first half of this year.

In a statement, he said that the new cost-cutting plans were “a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group”.

“We are taking responsibility for our entire workforce, for our partners and for industrial jobs worldwide,” he added.

data.title: Hugo Boss chairman quits amid Mike Ashley power struggle
data.description:
The chairman of Hugo Boss has quit after Mike Ashley ramped up efforts to acquire the German fashion giant.

Stephan Sturm, who has been in the role for just over a year, will step down once a successor has been found, Mr Ashley’s Frasers Group said on Monday.

Robert Palmer, one of the billionaire tycoon’s key lieutenants, will join Hugo Boss’s board, where Mr Ashley’s son-in-law Michael Murray already holds a seat.

Hugo Boss’s board rejected a £1.7bn takeover offer from Frasers in July. This led Frasers to build a stake in the company, resulting in the UK group owning 48pc of Hugo Boss.

Mr Ashley is planning to increase his stake beyond the 50pc mark to become a majority owner.

Frasers said Mr Sturm had “mutually agreed” to step down as chairman and leave the board.

It said: “Frasers would like to thank Mr Sturm for the contribution he has made to Hugo Boss as chairman of the supervisory board and intends to work with him in the future.”

Mr Ashley’s retail giant began building a stake in the German luxury brand in 2020, crossing the 30pc threshold earlier this year.

This automatically triggers a mandatory offer for the remaining business under German market rules.

The Sports Direct owner is eyeing a move into high-end retail, where a slowdown in the luxury sector has paved the way for deals.

The ousting of the chairman is another sign that Mr Ashley is tightening his grip on the German fashion maker, where Frasers is the largest shareholder by a wide margin.

Frasers previously said the offer was an opportunity to create “a stronger, more resilient and more successful” company.

Hugo Boss was founded in 1924 and became synonymous with corporate suits and premium men’s tailoring in the 1980s.

Frasers also owns shares in Mulberry and Burberry and recently bought Harvey Nichols in a pre-pack administration deal for £40m.

Mr Ashley is the 48th richest person in the UK, according to the Sunday Times Rich List, boasting a net worth of £3.44bn.

The billionaire left school without any qualifications before starting his retail empire with a sports and ski shop in Maidenhead.

data.title: Tesco’s dominance slips as rivals gain ground
data.description:
Tesco is losing its grip on the grocery market as rivals gain ground and food prices accelerate ahead of the Budget.

Industry figures seen by The Telegraph show Britain’s biggest supermarket shed market share over the summer, falling from 24.5pc a year ago to 24.1pc.

The chain also sold fewer products over the period, suggesting shoppers are buying less as household budgets come under pressure.

Tesco’s sales rose by 2.4pc, compared with 3.9pc across the grocery market as a whole.

By contrast, food sales at Marks & Spencer rose by 14.8pc over the 12 weeks to Sept 6, while Lidl grew by 8.2pc and Ocado by 14.2pc. M&S increased its grocery market share from 3.7pc to 4.1pc, while Lidl’s rose from 7.4pc to 7.7pc.

The figures come as food price inflation rose for the first time in six months. Grocery prices increased by 2.3pc in the four weeks ending on Sept 6, up from 2.1pc in August, according to the latest figures from Worldpanel.

It marked the first rise in food inflation since February’s peak of 4.3pc, after six months of steady decline.

The increase poses a risk to Mr Burnham, who has put lowering the cost of living at the centre of his policy platform since taking office in July, cutting VAT on electricity bills and capping bus fares.

However, shoppers have already been warned of a year of food price pain, with the Food and Drink Federation predicting price inflation to peak at 6.4pc next July.

The latest food price rises helped lift supermarkets sales by 2pc in the month ending Sept 6, according to Worldpanel.

Analysts said the rise in inflation would be likely to put pressure on retailers to keep competing on prices as customers rein in spending.

Mike Watkins, of retail research group NielsenIQ, said: “Following one of the hottest summers on record, which encouraged consumers to spend more freely, September is likely to mark a return to tighter household budgeting.

“With children now back at school, consumers are likely to enter a period of reassessing priorities, taking stock of finances, and monitoring spending more closely.”

Tesco was approached for comment.

data.title: Family TV time is dead ... and doomscrolling killed it
data.description:
The days of families gathering around the TV could soon be at an end, with young Britons increasingly glued to their own screens.

Almost half of the time (44pc) UK adults spend watching, reading or listening to commercial media is now spent alone, according to new figures from advertising trade body the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising (IPA).

That figure is 10 percentage points higher than in 2015. It means adults now spend just over two and a half hours consuming media on their own each day.

Solo viewing is most common among 16 to 34-year-olds, who spend 46pc of their media time in isolation, up by more than a fifth from a decade ago. That equates to two hours and 45 minutes per day.

Across all age groups, solo viewing time is considerably higher for men than women.

The shift in viewing habits comes amid an explosion of choice for British consumers, who can now take their pick from a plethora of streaming and on-demand options rather than a narrow choice of TV channels and radio stations.

It has led to a fragmentation in the way media is consumed, with younger audiences particularly isolated. It has also resulted in a drop in the number of shared cultural moments.

Among all UK adults, smartphones now account for the same share of commercial media time as TV sets – 34pc.

However, smartphones represent 49pc of viewing time among 16 to 34-year-olds. This comes despite growing concerns over habits such as “doomscrolling”. The TV viewing among younger audiences has fallen from 32pc in 2015 to 21pc in 2026.

Just under half the time young people spend viewing commercial media is on apps such as TikTok, Instagram or YouTube.

Meanwhile, the time adults spend talking face-to-face per day is down by 4pc from 2015 to seven hours and 25 minutes. For 16 to 34-year-olds, it is down 11pc to seven hours and 10 minutes.

Simon Frazier, of the IPA, said: “Consider a Saturday night in a family home in the late 1980s and everyone would possibly be glued to Beadle’s About, sharing anecdotes and bonding over a shared experience.

“Compare that to today, when the likelihood is that the family will be on multiple screens in different rooms of the house. The shared media experience is increasingly under pressure.”

The figures highlight the challenge facing traditional broadcasters as viewers defect to online entertainment.

Commercial broadcasters such as ITV and Channel 4 are grappling with falling advertising revenues, while the BBC, which is funded by the licence fee and therefore not included in the IPA’s data, was overtaken by YouTube in audience numbers for the first time this year.

Despite the shift to solo viewing, streaming giants such as Netflix have been experimenting with traditional TV formats such as live events and weekly schedules in an effort to create shared moments to boost their fledgling advertising efforts.

Farhann Cachra, of Global, the media group behind radio stations LBC and Classic FM, said: “Personalisation risks becoming isolation, and with it an atomised society and a propensity to feed an individualised culture.

“At the same time, the human need for collective experience hasn’t shrunk, it’s just been squeezed into fewer moments. That scarcity is precisely what makes them so valuable.”

data.title: Even The Canary doesn’t deserve to be debanked
data.description:
Is another wave of debanking underway?

The Leftist news site The Canary reports that it has had two bank accounts frozen and that it now has no choice but to suspend its operation altogether. Many will be delighted that The Canary has stopped publishing – but you don’t have to support the platform to worry about the power that banks now exercise over our free speech and free press. The Canary’s shutdown should be a wake-up call to us all.

The Canary claims it was given no forewarning, no explanation and no opportunity to challenge the initial decision by Lloyds to freeze its account in June, just two weeks after it expanded into printing editions for newsagents. Now, the outlet reports that Metro Bank has frozen another account associated with the company, leaving them unable to operate.

Coutts’ debanking of Nigel Farage in 2023 was perhaps the most high-profile example of political debanking but it’s far from the only one. Before Farage’s account closure, in 2020 Barclays closed two accounts associated with a Christian charity Core Issues Trust after it was the target of a LGBT social-media campaign against conversion therapy. Muslim organisations have long reported debanking issues, with waves of account closures over years.

The investigation that followed the Farage debanking scandal showed his was not an isolated case. It examined 84 other accounts of “politically exposed” people that had been closed by NatWest around the same time – a 10 per cent sample of relevant closures. NatWest, which owns Coutts, initially claimed that Farage’s sudden account closure had nothing to do with the Reform leader’s political views. However, documents showed senior staff had internally complained about his “xenophobic, chauvinistic and racist views” and deemed them to be “at odds with our position” before his account was closed.

Corporations are entitled to their relentless, insufferable position-taking, flag-waving and ethics-washing and they are entitled to choose or lose customers as they like – but under the Equality Act 2010, they cannot discriminate against people for their race, religion, sexuality or indeed most political views. Fair and equal treatment is a very fundamental principle in English law – and we ought to be equally alarmed by political debanking whoever it might target.

I couldn’t find any records of The Canary writing about, let alone raising the alarm about, Farage’s debanking. The Left and Right silos of concern about our country’s mounting censorship problem are part of the reason it has been able to reach such a crisis point. And now, Canary staff members arguably find themselves in an even worse position than Farage. The Canary’s direct debits have bounced, temporarily taking its website offline; projects have been cancelled, invoices can’t be settled, and staff can’t be paid.

Censorship by debanking has not just a financial cost, nor just a democratic cost, but a significant human cost too. That’s why it’s so powerful. Few people are so determined to express their most unpopular opinions that they will risk their livelihoods to do it.

George Galloway claimed this week that he can’t pay his mortgage, can’t pay his tax bill and can’t care for his 92-year-old mother as he too has just been debanked. The Workers Party of Britain leader says he was a customer of the Bank of Scotland – part of the Lloyds Banking Group – for 39 years before his account was closed without forewarning or explanation.

Banks insist account closures are never politically driven, but people and organisations sharing remarkably similar politics seem to have their accounts frozen around the same time.

The banks might have entirely legitimate reasons for closing The Canary and Galloway’s bank accounts. But their refusal to tell their customers why accounts have been shut down doesn’t suggest so. It is understandable, for privacy reasons, that the banks don’t talk about these cases to the public, but if they’d had the decency to talk to the account owners before their financial executions, they could at least reassure the public that they had provided their reasoning privately.

Instead, the banks’ silence speaks volumes. It shows their total indifference to the damage they are inflicting on our freedom of speech and freedom of the press.

In the absence of any explanation, The Canary and Galloway are prompted to speculate about why they have been targeted. Is it a conspiracy against their pro-Palestine views? Is it the national security apparatus manoeuvring against them? Are they such a threat to the establishment?

The answer seems to be that banks associate politics with risk and are constantly seeking to “de-risk”. But we need to stop treating controversial opinions as a risk. They are a feature, not a flaw, of a living, breathing democracy.

data.title: Ignore rising factory costs at your peril, Ford boss warns Labour
data.description:
Labour ignores rising energy, tax and regulatory costs “at our peril”, Ford’s UK chief has warned, amid fears of a fresh raid on business.

Lisa Brankin said the car giant’s British operations were already under heavy pressure, forcing the company to work “really hard to make sure that we keep what we’ve got”.

Speaking to The Telegraph during a tour of Ford’s Dagenham plant, she said: “I think we neglect the cost issue at our peril, if we think that new jobs will stay here irrespective of cost.”

Her comments represent the latest warning from Britain’s beleaguered automotive industry after the decision by Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) to cut 4,000 jobs and come as John Healey, the Chancellor, is reportedly mulling more tax rises to plug a hole in the public finances.

Ms Brankin pointed to recent increases to National Insurance contributions and business rates, high industrial electricity prices and the Government’s electric vehicle (EV) targets as examples of costs that were squeezing companies.

She said: “There’s a point where that comes back to bite you and I think we’re seeing the cost – the cost of energy in particular in the UK – becoming really, really challenging.

“I don’t think we’re alone in that, in terms of industry that would say.”

Ms Brankin said Ford’s UK operations would be difficult to replicate elsewhere and that its workforce was highly skilled and efficient but admitted “there are certainly cheaper places to operate”.

Ford builds some 600,000 diesel engines per year at its Dagenham plant, including for the Ranger Super Duty pickup truck and its popular Transit vans, although this represents just half of the historic site’s capacity.

It also makes crankshafts, engine blocks and cylinder heads there.

As part of an effort to secure a £900m contract from the Ministry of Defence to replace the Army’s fleet of Land Rovers, Ford has said the Dagenham plant could also supply engines for a militarised version of the Ranger.

The base chassis would be made in Thailand with final assembly and modifications taking place in Britain.

Ms Brankin suggested on Monday that the Ranger was an “off-the-peg” candidate that was cost-effective and required minimal modifications.

She added: “There’s no development required on these vehicles. They’re already in production.

“We sell Rangers around the world. We build over 300,000 every year, so it’s there and it’s ready.”

Other carmakers bidding for the contract include JLR, General Motors, Babcock, Ineos and the start-up Fering.

Ford is separately investing £380m in an upgrade of its factory in Halewood, Merseyside, where it is transitioning from making gearboxes to drive units for EVs.

‘Hoping to see change’

However, the company is lobbying the Government to relax the requirements of the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which sets targets that carmakers must meet for sales of electric cars and vans.

Ford and other carmakers have argued that the targets are too far ahead of consumer demand. If they fail to meet them, they face the prospect of hefty fines.

Asked about the effect on future investment of the mandate and rising costs, Ms Brankin replied: “Everything has an effect on how you look at the UK, which is one of the reasons we’ve been so vociferous in calling for a review of the ZEV mandate.

“Fortunately, the Government just launched its consultation, so we’re hoping to see some change there.

“We’re not looking at it in terms of our business case here, but just thinking about the viability of the business overall.”

The chief executive added: “The transition to EVs is something that we’ve bought into, that we’ve invested really heavily in.

“All we’re concerned about is the pace of change that’s being forced, and that it’s so out of kilter with customer demand, and that’s putting a lot of pressure on our business.”

The Government was approached for comment.

data.title: ‘Can’t-build’ Britain has become a global embarrassment
data.description:
The next time you find yourself with too much time on your hands, type “Chinese mega-projects” into YouTube or TikTok. I promise you won’t be disappointed.

Social media is awash with fascinating videos celebrating the pace at which China’s hyper-efficient and highly skilled engineers are able to complete massive construction projects.

Some have millions of views, like a 90-second time-lapse of a 57-storey skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan Province in southern China being built in just 19 days.

Sir Pascal Soriot, the AstraZeneca boss and an unabashed Sinophile, is among those who now talk about “China speed”: the sort of rapid execution that has enabled its car industry to go from laggard to clear frontrunner in less than a decade.

Ditto the way Chinese pharmaceutical and biotech industries, once dismissed as little more than providers of cheap copycat pills, are now at the forefront of life-changing drug discovery.

While China erects apartment buildings, emergency hospitals and bridges in days, Britain – a country whose Victorian forefathers were once the envy of the engineering world – seems to have almost stopped building things.

Virtually every genuinely transformative piece of infrastructure that is proposed either gets stuck in the planning system or is derailed by yet more short-sighted Nimbyism.

The few projects that do get off the ground are delayed for years as costs balloon and everyone squabbles about who should foot the bill.

Yet, as argued in an extensive report from the private-sector-led Public Private Partnership Commission, led by Sir John Armitt, it doesn’t have to be this way.

The study starts off with a sobering reminder of how the UK hasn’t built a reservoir since 1992. It could have chosen multiple other examples, such as the fact that there hasn’t been a nuclear plant constructed in three decades or how we’ve been debating a third runway at Heathrow Airport for a quarter of a century.

At the same time, the roads are falling apart, our prisons are buckling and Ofwat has warned that population growth and climate change could leave England facing a water deficit of billions of litres a day within the next 25 years.

One of the biggest problems the UK faces is levels of bureaucracy that at times wouldn’t have looked out of place in China before it became a market economy at the end of the 90s.

Britain’s sclerotic planning and regulatory regime is a curse, sharply pushing up costs and delivery time, which is a massive turn-off to private investors who are going to become increasingly vital as the nation’s stretched finances make it harder to fund vital projects.

Sir John’s findings are genuinely alarming and should shame the bureaucrats that impede progress at every possible turn.

The UK’s pre-construction phase alone averages 65 months. In China, they managed to build the Danyang-Kunshan Bridge – the world’s longest at more than 102 miles – in less time.

Meanwhile, the average time required to secure development consent for nationally significant projects in Britain doubled between 2009 and 2019, and delivery schedules jumped 65pc between 2012 and 2021.

Comparisons with other countries are enough to make you weep.

Analysis by Bradshaw Advisory, a consultancy, of more than 5,000 projects around the world worth more than $1bn (£750m) found that UK projects take an average of almost 12 and a half years from announcement to completion – the second-longest period of any high-to-middle-income country.

Unsurprisingly, this leaves us paying a huge premium: road construction costs are at least 20pc higher than in comparable countries, nuclear power plants cost approximately 50pc more and rail costs twice as much.

Amid such embarrassing delays, the chances of finding the estimated £258bn required to modernise Britain with new reservoirs, prisons and schools between now and the end of the decade seem remote at best.

We already have the lowest levels of investment in the G7. A separate Oxford Economics report found that the UK had lagged every major economy except Greece for investment for the past 25 years.

As the commission points out, it’s not as if this critical infrastructure can be funded with additional borrowing when the public finances are already at breaking point. With the tax burden at a post-Second World War high, higher taxes are not a realistic option either. That leaves Britain having to go cap in hand to pension funds and overseas investors.

There’s certainly no shortage of untapped money sloshing around the financial system with more than £1tn in private defined-benefit schemes, another £1.2tn in defined-contribution schemes and almost £400bn to be found in local government pensions.

Yet the average allocation for infrastructure among defined-contribution schemes is just 3pc in the UK, compared with roughly 14pc among their Australian counterparts.

For the UK to attract the private capital required, there first needs to be a total overhaul of the sclerotic planning and regulatory regime – and for this to occur, Whitehall needs to overcome its aversion to risk, the commission argues.

This is where its findings really strike a chord. The UK is obsessed with consultations, white papers and judicial reviews.

The political and institutional mindset is one that seeks to erect barriers, not tear them down. There is an industry of lobbyists, accountants, lawyers and other overpaid advisers who stand to make a fortune from obfuscation. Nimbys, activists and other minority groups have too much power to influence decisions too.

Heathrow Airport’s plans for a third runway have been through the High Court, the Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court and despite receiving backing from Gordon Brown’s government, Theresa May’s and Sir Keir Starmer’s, they are still awaiting planning consent. It is a national disgrace.

The commission also points to the damning findings of the Nuclear Regulatory Taskforce, which blamed a culture that favoured process over outcome for making Britain the most expensive place in the world to build a nuclear plant, as well as a regulatory regime whose default position was “the most cautious available reading of their own rules”.

To the commission’s great credit, it proposes a series of major changes that could break the logjam, including a requirement for all so-called arm’s-length bodies such as Natural England to be supportive of economic growth.

The most striking proposal it makes is the creation of an independent institution for infrastructure with “credibility comparable to the Office for Budget Responsibility” that reports to Parliament, not ministers.

Projects deemed to be of critical national importance would be put to a “parliamentary confirmatory vote” once Parliament has endorsed them, to reduce the threat of what Sir John calls the “horrible merry-go-round” of legal challenges.

The need for more radical thinking has never been more urgent.

Britain is stuck in a low-to-no-growth trap that stretches back to the global financial crisis nearly two decades ago and it is destined to become more severe, not less. Solving it should be a national emergency.

data.title: 100-year-old construction giant to stop building homes in UK
data.description:
A 100-year-old construction giant will halt housebuilding to focus on road and hospital projects, as the property slump continues to take its toll on the sector.

FTSE 250 builder Kier Group said on Tuesday that from 2027 “there will be no investment in new property developments, with capital reallocated to enhance the group’s balance sheet strength”.

Its portfolio includes more than 5,000 homes, with construction under way on seven sites. It has said it will finish these before exiting property development.

Stuart Togwell, the chief executive, said the property group was taking “important steps to strengthen and simplify the business”.

Kier will instead focus on its infrastructure and construction divisions, citing more growth opportunities.

In particular, the company is expecting “significant revenue growth” from its water, energy, defence and healthcare contracts.

One of Britain’s biggest construction groups, Kier designs and builds various projects, including schools, hospitals, highways, energy projects and waterworks.

These include roles on HS2 and the Sizewell C nuclear power station.

A £55m office in Liverpool and a 9,290 sq m warehousing site in Manchester are also among its existing property developments.

The news will deal a setback to Labour’s manifesto pledge to build 1.5 million homes during this parliament – a target thsat Angela Rayner, the Housing Secretary, admitted on Sunday that the Government had a “slim chance” of reaching.

Construction continues to suffer a slump amid persistently high inflation, rising build costs and weak housebuyer demand.

Housebuilder MJ Gleeson swung to a loss and cut jobs on Tuesday as the housing gloom continued to take its toll.

MJ Gleeson made a £2.7m loss in the year ending June 30, blaming “subdued” demand for housing. This compared with a £20.5m profit in the prior year.

Graham Prothero, the chief executive, said demand for homes had been hit by an 11-year high in homes for sale in England, rising mortgage rates, and increasing cost of living pressures.

Mr Prothero added that taxes and red tape were making it harder to build homes profitably. The burdens include a building-safety levy to pay for cladding remediation and new net zero rules.

“It is in the gift of this Government to put the brakes on some of those things,” he said. “Now is a very bad time to be imposing the new building safety levy on us ... and the future home regulations [are coming] next year.

“Do we need to do that right now? Could we postpone that and ease the viability challenge? It would be great if we could get some help in that regard.”

The cost of building a new home has risen by £76,000 since 2020, according to the Home Builders Federation. Mr Prothero said half of this was because of increased taxes and regulation.

Under a restructuring at the housebuilder, the company shed 21 jobs after making 56 redundancies while creating 35 jobs.

The group also shut its East Yorkshire office, pulled out of 12 development sites that it had bought and combined its Greater Manchester and Cumbria operations.

Its housing land pipeline has fallen from 19,638 to 14,927 plots.

Mr Prothero said that the “subdued market may not improve any time soon”, so it was taking a “prudent stance” on managing its cash flows. The builder sold 1,968 homes during the year, up 10pc from the previous year.

“You shouldn’t get the impression there are no buyers out there; there absolutely are,” he said. “And we are focusing on what we can do better in order to win over those buyers.”

data.title: Richard Branson’s plan to make the Eurostar feel like a second-class service
data.description:
Sir Richard Branson’s much touted plan to bring some of the glamour of Virgin Atlantic to his own version of the Eurostar has been derided as a pipe dream by critics.

Overcrowding at St Pancras, a chronic lack of suitable train-maintenance sites and the inevitable mountain of red tape have been viewed as almost insurmountable obstacles to anyone intent on ending Eurostar’s monopoly over services through the Channel tunnel.

But after securing permission to run 20 trains a day between London and the Continent from Britain’s rail regulator, the billionaire’s Virgin Trains is finally beginning to win over doubters.

Virgin must still negotiate access to the tunnel itself, as well as tracks in France, Belgium and the Netherlands. And it faces a nervous wait for a fleet of 12 as yet untested high-speed trains on order from manufacturer Alstom.

However, a ruling from regulators at the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) last week suggests Sir Richard may be about to make good on his ambition of returning to Britain’s railways after Virgin Trains lost the West Coast Main Line franchise in 2019.

Virgin Trains is not the only operator intent on challenging Eurostar’s 31-year monopoly.

Italy’s state-owned Trenitalia announced earlier this month a €2bn (£1.7bn) order for 19 new trains, around half of which it aims to deploy on Channel tunnel services, while a clutch of other would-be operators are also drawing up proposals.

If those plans come to fruition, competition on the route could explode within five years, which could have an impact matching that of the 1990s discount-airline boom.

Plunging fares may encourage an influx of new customers and further loosen the grip of airlines on routes such as London to Paris, where Eurostar already has 80pc of the market.

Train services from London are likely to reach further into Europe, with lower ticket prices making rail competitive as far as Germany, Switzerland and even Italy for travellers with time on their hands.

Mark Smith, a former ORR and Department for Transport executive who runs the Man in Seat 61 travel website, reckons ticket prices could drop by close to a third.

“You’d be looking at more capacity, higher service standards and fares that could be 30pc lower based on what we have seen with the advent of competition in Italy and Spain,” he says.

“That will in turn drive further market share gains for rail compared with the airlines and make it feasible to travel further into Europe on a single ticket.”

Customer service front and centre

Virgin has so far been tight-lipped on what the Channel tunnel service might look like, with Phil Whittingham, its project lead, saying only that the route is “ripe for change” and that Sir Richard intended to build a “premium customer experience on board”.

A spokesman adds: “We don’t want to ruin the element of surprise, but just as we’ve done with Virgin Atlantic and our holidays and hotels offering, you can expect bold ideas with the customer experience front and centre.”

On Virgin Atlantic, that experience has included in-flight bar and massages, with a shift to focusing on tech innovation in recent years, including free Wi-Fi from Elon Musk’s Starlink and an AI-powered virtual concierge.

Virgin has specified single-decker trains for its purchase from Alstom, with one insider suggesting that they were more compatible with providing a full at-seat meal service than the double-deckers with which Eurostar is renewing its fleet.

Virgin has said it intends to operate an initial six return trains a day between London and Paris starting in October 2030, later increasing to 13, followed by four to Brussels and three to Amsterdam.

That would represent a substantial increase on the current timetable, with Eurostar offering 14 daily services to Paris, eight or nine to Brussels and five to Amsterdam.

The company, owned by French state railway SNCF, said Virgin’s plan confirmed “the huge potential for growth in international rail” and that it intended to “play a full part in that growth”.

Jon Worth, an expert in European railways, says Virgin had impressed with its work to secure access to St Pancras, the line to the tunnel and the last remaining space at Temple Mills maintenance shed near Stratford before Trenitalia.

“Seeing this project through has been like threading the eye of a needle,” he adds. “Forget the rhetoric from Branson about transforming travel. They’ve been very methodical and very clear headed in devising a project that will just about fit with all these restrictions.”

No room for slippage

However, he says Virgin had taken a risk in choosing a bespoke version of a train built by Alstom in Italy which has not yet been approved in France, introducing the “nightmare” scenario of the trains not being ready for 2030.

Any slippage could open the door to Trenitalia, which is viewed as among the most aggressive of European high-speed operators.

Trenitalia’s train order, from Hitachi Rail, adds to an existing commitment with the Japanese manufacturer and will provide guaranteed delivery times, potentially beating Virgin to the market by a year.

Worth says Trenitalia is likely to expand on routes such as Paris to Lyon and Marseilles and Milan, rather than focusing on London.

Eurostar’s switch to double-deckers for an order of up to 50 new trains may also be problematic, he adds, since the Celestia model is not currently compliant with evacuation requirements within the tunnel in the event of fire.

It is likely that a significant number of the new trains will instead be used on the Paris-Brussels route that Eurostar took over in 2022, easing the pressure on Virgin.

Waiting in the wings are Evolyn, backed by Spanish industrialist Jorge Cosmen, an investor in the owner of National Express, the Dutch startup Heuro, and UK-based Gemini, which has proposed running trains from Stratford and Ebbsfleet to avoid the St Pancras bottleneck.

According to Smith, of the Man in Seat 61 website, Virgin’s best bet will be to play to its strengths by offering upmarket food and wine, exploring initiatives such as allowing carriage of bicycles and dogs, which is currently banned from most Eurostar services.

He says: “It’s that hard-to-define Virgin pizazz that people most want to see and they’ll need to bring that to these trains.”

data.title: Founder of collapsed shadow bank ‘gambled millions at Mayfair casinos’
data.description:
The founder of a collapsed British shadow bank spent millions in Mayfair’s casinos.

Paresh Raja, who led Market Financial Solutions (MFS), was a prolific gambler at two prominent Mayfair casinos, the Palm Beach Casino and the Colony Club, according to an individual familiar with Mr Raja’s gambling.

MFS collapsed earlier this year amid accusations of a £1.3bn fraud.

Mr Raja and his wife allegedly received more than £408m from “funds managed by MFS” to “personal bank accounts” in the UK, Monaco, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates, according to a separate lawsuit made on behalf of some of the shadow bank’s creditors.

He is also accused of buying “a vast number of cars” including three Aston Martins, two Mercedes, six Ferraris and three Rolls-Royces.

Mr Raja and his wife deny wrongdoing and have consistently maintained that there was no fraud or dishonesty.

According to an individual familiar with Mr Raja’s gambling, the founder would regularly bet up to £60,000 a spin on roulette tables and had a debit card approved by the casinos to be drawn down up to £600,000 per day to gamble with.

This was unusual even by the standards of casinos in Mayfair. As the UK emerged from lockdown, Mr Raja had nearly £1m deposited with the casinos in Mayfair, which were owned by Genting, a Malaysian conglomerate.

The conglomerate has more than 50 casinos in three continents, many of which are in the UK, it has also diversified into other activities including power generation and plantations.

The individual familiar with Mr Raja’s gambling said: “He would come in midweek with a couple of guys that worked with him. These were nice chaps but sort of flunkies, sycophants, let-the-boss-win-at-golf kind of thing.

“He would play and play, drink and drink, and if he didn’t lose all his money at the Palm Beach, he would then get in a car and go around the corner to the Colony Club.”

MFS fell into administration in February, triggering allegations that at least £1.3bn has been “misappropriated” from the business.

Mr Raja was hit by a worldwide freezing order earlier this year, which barred him from spending more than £5,000 a week without creditors’ consent.

The company described itself as a specialist provider of buy-to-let mortgage lending and bridging finance.

It was part of a fast-growing crop of so-called bridging lenders in the UK. These firms provide short-term, property-backed loans to borrowers who may not qualify for traditional bank financing. They often charge higher interest rates.

The property lender boasted a loan book of roughly £2.5bn as of last March and its customers spanned the breadth of the UK.

Its clients included property investors and overseas family offices as well as prominent businessmen and celebrities in Britain.

It was also a shadow bank, which meant it funded its loans by borrowing from banks and other lenders.

The company’s creditors included Barclays, Santander, Wells Fargo and Jefferies. Private capital firms including Apollo’s Atlas SP Partners and Castlelake also extended financing to the failed mortgage lender.

A spokesman for Mr Raja said: “Mr Raja will not comment on a personal vilification campaign.”

Genting was contacted for comment.

data.title: Labour to nationalise one of UK’s biggest steelworks
data.description:
Labour is to nationalise one of Britain’s biggest steelworks after talks to find a private-sector buyer collapsed.

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, said Speciality Steel UK (SSUK) was at risk of closure “by default” without ministers intervening.

Its demise would have meant the loss of 1,300 jobs across its sites in Rotherham, Stocksbridge and Brinsworth in Yorkshire, and Wednesbury in the Midlands.

The company – previously owned by Sanjeev Gupta, the metals tycoon – has been in the hands of the official receiver for the last year while talks to find a buyer have taken place.

Officials had been in advanced talks with Blastr, a Norwegian start-up, but Mr Reynolds said the Government had decided the potential buyer’s request for state support did not represent good value for money, ruling it out on Monday.

That meant the only way to prevent SSUK’s imminent collapse was to take it into public ownership, he said.

The Government said the takeover would be funded “from existing budgets” but did not disclose how much, if anything, it would pay for the business. Mr Reynolds said due diligence processes were ongoing.

Continuing to run the business will cost taxpayers. Staff wages alone at the company’s plant in Rotherham, South Yorkshire, have been costing the official receiver £4m per month.

As part of the nationalisation, SSUK’s electric arc furnace, mothballed for months, is poised to restart in December.

Mr Reynolds said SSUK had “specialist capabilities” with “strategic value” beyond its contribution to the economy. The company previously made aircraft landing gear, helicopter rotors and components for missiles and artillery shells.

It is also a supplier to oil and gas, automotive and engineering businesses.

Mr Reynolds told MPs: “We can allow events to take their course through the liquidation process and risk being left with no say in the future of these sites, or we can act. This Government chooses to act.

“It would not be right to let this go by default.”

Blastr said it was “disappointed” by the decision and insisted its offer would have carried “no cost to the British taxpayer”.

The move represents Labour’s latest state intervention in Britain’s steel industry, with the Government now in control of more than half of the country’s total output.

Ministers also stepped in to seize control of British Steel from its Chinese owner last year, after separately handing £500m to Tata Steel to support a green overhaul of its plant in South Wales.

SSUK went into liquidation last year after Mr Gupta’s main lender, Greensill Capital, collapsed in 2021. Since then, the Government has been trying to find a buyer.

The company melts down scrap using an electric arc furnace and supplies highly engineered steel to the aerospace and defence industry, although its melting operations have been on hold. SSUK’s steel-rolling mills have been operational during the liquidation process.

Mr Reynolds said officials had sought a private-sector suitor for the business and identified a preferred buyer but ministers had ruled out providing the support package the bidder requested.

“We have serious concerns about the proposed financing of it, the protections for UK taxpayers and whether it would be able to offer long-term stability for the local economy and community,” he added.

The Government would “therefore engage with the official receiver’s sales process and develop a proposal for the public acquisition of SSUK”, he said.

However, Mr Reynolds added that nationalisation was “not the end of the process”.

He said: “It means keeping our options open.

“Working towards public acquisition will create the necessary time and space to undertake a full assessment of the opportunities available.”

The decision to nationalise the plant was welcomed by industry group UK Steel, which said it would help to “release much of the pressure” on the domestic supply of key steel categories.

Gareth Stace, UK Steel’s director general, said: “SSUK is already well on its way to returning to full operations and retaking its place at the heart of critical UK supply chains.

“It is crucial that the custodian of this key strategic asset is the right owner and investor, with the expertise and long-term ambition that the dedicated workforce deserves.”

data.title: Founder of collapsed shadow bank ‘gambled millions at Mayfair casinos’
data.description:
The founder of a collapsed British shadow bank spent millions in Mayfair’s casinos.

Paresh Raja, who led Market Financial Solutions (MFS), was a prolific gambler at two prominent Mayfair casinos, the Palm Beach Casino and the Colony Club, according to an individual familiar with Mr Raja’s gambling.

MFS collapsed earlier this year amid accusations of a £1.3bn fraud.

Mr Raja and his wife allegedly received more than £408m from “funds managed by MFS” to “personal bank accounts” in the UK, Monaco, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates, according to a separate lawsuit made on behalf of some of the shadow bank’s creditors.

He is also accused of buying “a vast number of cars” including three Aston Martins, two Mercedes, six Ferraris and three Rolls-Royces.

Mr Raja and his wife deny wrongdoing and have consistently maintained that there was no fraud or dishonesty.

According to an individual familiar with Mr Raja’s gambling, the founder would regularly bet up to £60,000 a spin on roulette tables and had a debit card approved by the casinos to be drawn down up to £600,000 per day to gamble with.

This was unusual even by the standards of casinos in Mayfair. As the UK emerged from lockdown, Mr Raja had nearly £1m deposited with the casinos in Mayfair, which were owned by Genting, a Malaysian conglomerate.

The conglomerate has more than 50 casinos in three continents, many of which are in the UK, it has also diversified into other activities including power generation and plantations.

The individual familiar with Mr Raja’s gambling said: “He would come in midweek with a couple of guys that worked with him. These were nice chaps but sort of flunkies, sycophants, let-the-boss-win-at-golf kind of thing.

“He would play and play, drink and drink, and if he didn’t lose all his money at the Palm Beach, he would then get in a car and go around the corner to the Colony Club.”

MFS fell into administration in February, triggering allegations that at least £1.3bn has been “misappropriated” from the business.

Mr Raja was hit by a worldwide freezing order earlier this year, which barred him from spending more than £5,000 a week without creditors’ consent.

The company described itself as a specialist provider of buy-to-let mortgage lending and bridging finance.

It was part of a fast-growing crop of so-called bridging lenders in the UK. These firms provide short-term, property-backed loans to borrowers who may not qualify for traditional bank financing. They often charge higher interest rates.

The property lender boasted a loan book of roughly £2.5bn as of last March and its customers spanned the breadth of the UK.

Its clients included property investors and overseas family offices as well as prominent businessmen and celebrities in Britain.

It was also a shadow bank, which meant it funded its loans by borrowing from banks and other lenders.

The company’s creditors included Barclays, Santander, Wells Fargo and Jefferies. Private capital firms including Apollo’s Atlas SP Partners and Castlelake also extended financing to the failed mortgage lender.

A spokesman for Mr Raja said: “Mr Raja will not comment on a personal vilification campaign.”

Genting was contacted for comment.
