data.title: Sandbanks residents fight plans to bulldoze historic hotel
data.description:
Sandbanks residents are fighting plans to bulldoze a historic hotel.

The Haven Hotel has stood at the entrance to Poole Harbour in Dorset since 1880, and was one of the first properties to be built on the peninsula.

Once the home of Guglielmo Marconi, credited with inventing the wireless telegraph system, the four-storey building has been a landmark for passing yachts, pleasure boats and cross-Channel ferries ever since.

But the owners of the 84-room hotel are seeking planning permission to demolish it, raising concerns that a building of historical importance is falling foul of property developers.

Keith Ulyatt, a resident, wrote in his letter of objection: “Granting permission for demolition without any proposal of what is to replace it is totally unacceptable.

“It raises the prospect of a flattened empty building plot being in place for years, in the most iconic of local locations... so that any subsequent proposed building would be acceptable compared to the wasteland created.”

Andrew Reed wrote: “This application is nothing short of vandalism, a ploy to avoid the rigorous assessment of a future development application by reducing a useable and valuable asset to a piece of waste ground in the most prominent of locations.”

Sarah Charles added: “The Haven Hotel in Sandbanks should not be demolished. It is a site of significant heritage, and is a wonderful hotel in the present day.

“It was once home to Marconi, who conducted important work for wireless telegraphy, and is an icon of 1920s architecture. It would be an act of vandalism on this iconic Sandbanks landmark if it were to be demolished.”

Marconi, an electrical engineer from Italy, came to England to prove that radio waves could travel long distances. 

He settled at the Haven Hotel in 1898 to conduct his experiments and built a 120ft transmitter mast in the hotel grounds.

Operators on the Titanic used Marconi’s radio network to transmit their SOS emergency signals in April 2012.

Richard Carr, of Property Planning Strategy, who is working on behalf of FJB Hotels, the owner, said the hotel could not be saved in its present form but insisted that a new hotel, as opposed to residential flats, would be built on the site.

“The site has to be used as a hotel, and we plan to submit a new application very soon for an 85-bedroom hotel,” he said. “We are planning to demolish the Haven, which isn’t listed or in a conservation area.

“The building has come to the end of its life. The majority of it is a steel-form building which faces the sea and has been exposed to salt water and south-westerly winds for over 100 years. Parts of it are severely corroded.

“If you run a bath, you get yellow water from where the pipes were made of galvanised steel that has perished over the years.

“The running costs that are just eye-watering and ridiculous. There are people jumping up and down and making noise about what will happen to the site, but if they read the local planning policy then they will see that we have to replace it with another hotel.”

Residents of Sandbanks, which consists of 800 households, include Harry Redknapp and Graeme Souness, the former footballers and football managers, and Sir Peter Ogden, the computer magnate.

data.title: Lime withdraws bikes from London borough after complaints from blind residents
data.description:
Lime has removed its electric bikes from a London borough after the company’s vehicles were accused of endangering blind residents.

The company said it had stopped users from being able to hire e-bikes in Bromley, south-east London, where it was operating without an agreement.

It came after Jason Beal, a resident, said he had had to force his guide dog into a busy road because of the company’s lime green bikes being strewn over the pavement.

Councillors had also threatened to pull Lime’s bikes off the streets and charge the company for the hassle.

Liam Conlon, the area’s MP, raised the matter with Bromley council after Mr Beal contacted him to complain.

Lime’s e-bikes have become ubiquitous in London and a popular way of getting around, but the hundreds of them parked on pavements have been seen by critics as a nuisance.

The company had started offering e-bike hire in the Bromley suburb of Penge in recent weeks, despite not having local approval. 

Lime put this down to a technical issue in which the map for neighbouring Lewisham mistakenly covered parts of Bromley. Councillors said they had “blighted” local areas and caused hazards on pavements.

Simon Fawthrop, of Bromley council, said: “We have already raised concerns with Lime that they appear to be operating without our consent in part of our borough.

“Bromley council have long had misgivings about Lime Bikes and other similar bikes that are quite frankly blighting some areas, where they are strewn across pavements causing multiple hazards.

“The council has not agreed anything with Lime and we call upon them to remove their bikes from our borough forthwith.”

Mr Beal, 53, told the London Standard that bikes parked on the pavement meant he had to walk on the road and listen out for traffic, frightening Caine, his guide dog.

“There have been a number of times the Lime bikes have been parked up or propped up against the tree or left over the pavement,” he said.

“So I’ve got to make a decision to try to take him into the main road. That’s a very frightening experience for myself.”

Lime was recently valued at $1.7bn (£1.3bn) in a US initial public offering.

The company operates bikes and scooters in more than a dozen London boroughs.

It has been blighted by claims of personal injuries caused by the bikes, and said recently that it had set aside $56m for personal injury claims.

Lime apologised to Mr Beal and said that it had suspended bike hiring in the borough until it could agree an approach “with appropriate parking locations”.

data.title: Zoe Ball’s Greatest Hits debut is another shot across Radio 2’s bow
data.description:
Two and a bit hours into Zoe Ball’s debut on Greatest Hits Radio, and it seemed that her former employer, the British Broadcasting Corporation, would not get anything more than a vague sideways mention. There were fleeting references to the “other station” from listeners, while Ball mentioned to her guest, actor Hugh Jackman, that he had also been her first visitor on a previous show (it was the Radio 2 Breakfast Show). Ball is generally on her best behaviour these days. And then, during one of the station’s typically bombastic stings, a wry voice-over came in: “They might have Cox, but we’ve got Ball”. Shots fired!

Ball now makes up a rather formidable daytime roster on the burgeoning commercial station, with Zoe Ball in the Afternoon (a deliberate nod to the late Steve Wright) sandwiched between Ken Bruce’s mid-morning programme and The Simon Mayo Drivetime Show. Nine hours of former Radio 2 DJs – and not any old Radio 2 DJs – every weekday. It would have been unthinkable 10 years ago, but the BBC’s grip on the airwaves is slipping year by year. Commercial radio now accounts for more than 55 per cent of British radio listening. A decade ago, it was 45 per cent.

However, unlike Bruce and Mayo, who both huffed off from the BBC in high dudgeon, Ball’s approach is nothing but sunshine and smiles. The Sara Cox/Zoe Ball quip aside, her first show was three hours of relentless, almost strenuous positivity, with the presenter calling everyone “gorgeous”, stating that she “loved” them and repeatedly using “I am obsessed with” when “I like” would have sufficed. None of this is a criticism. You come to Ball when you need cheering up, when you need relentless positivity and a shot of energy. The outside world is bleak. Stick Ball in your ears and it all goes away. The show’s vibe was summed up by another slogan, repeated several times: “The good times sound like this.” Cue Abba, Madonna, Fleetwood Mac.

The opening record, the Kiki Dee Band’s I’ve Got the Music in Me, was followed by a torrent of good-time bangers, carefully chosen to inspire desk dancing and to make you forget about masked men roaming around Dover or whatever other horrors we were informed about on the hour. Uncharacteristically, Ball sounded nervous, and admitted to as much during a first hour in which she kept tripping over her own tongue. Happily for her, this is commercial radio, so she had ample advert breaks to rein in the butterflies. Midway through, following a welcome laid-back appearance from the old charmer Jackman, Ball audibly relaxed. After that, she found her cruising gear.

“It’s just like the old days, isn’t it?” asked Mayo as he joined Ball for the 4pm handover. It is, Simon. Ball will fit in just nicely on Greatest Hits Radio, which will be delighted with its third coup and will presumably plot another.

The executives at Radio 2, meanwhile, will be watching Cox nervously.

Zoe Ball in the Afternoon is on Rayo and Greatest Hits Radio, weekdays at 1pm

data.title: Property magnate sues law firm for £180m over Spanish deal
data.description:
A British property magnate is suing one of Spain’s biggest law firms over claims its poor advice cost him €213m (£183m).

Edgeworth Capital, a Luxembourg fund owned by Robert Tchenguiz, is suing law firm Cuatrecasas in a dispute over the sale of Santander’s headquarters on the outskirts of Madrid.

Mr Tchenguiz bought the building as part of a €1.9bn deal in 2008. However, the vehicle he owned the property through fell into bankruptcy, and he ended up selling the property back to the bank for €3bn in 2019.

Cuatrecasas advised on the deal, but Edgeworth Capital alleges the law firm failed to properly advise it about two rulings in Spain’s Supreme Court that would have affected the value of the building.

These judgments limited creditors from claiming interest on certain debts. Mr Tchenguiz owned Santander’s headquarters through a company that had debts at the time covered by the ruling. Edgeworth argued that it undervalued the properties because it was unaware the judgments could limit its liability for these debts.

Mr Tchenguiz claims Edgeworth would have sought €426m more for Santander’s headquarters had it been aware of the rulings. Edgeworth would have been in line for 50pc of that “windfall” and it is now seeking to recover the €213m from Cuatrecasas through a High Court claim.

Cuatrecasas said Edgeworth wouldn’t have gained any benefit if it had been advised of the Supreme Court rulings. Lawyers for Cuatrecasas said: “Almost every aspect of [Edgeworth’s] pleaded case is in issue.”

After moving to Britain in 1979 to flee the Islamic revolution in Iran, Mr Tchenguiz built a property empire with Vincent Tchenguiz, his brother.

Mr Tchenguiz lives in the Royal College of Organists’ building in South Kensington, opposite the Royal Albert Hall. He once owned Shell-Mex House on London’s Victoria Embankment, before selling the building for £490m in 2007.

Mr Tchenguiz embarked on plans last year to launch an ultra-exclusive private members’ club in Mayfair called The Leconfield, supported by Liz Truss, the former prime minister. Leconfield House is the former headquarters of MI5, which he bought for £140m in 2004.

His father was an Iraqi-Jewish jeweller who fled persecution in Iraq by moving to Iran, before ending up in the Shah’s inner circle running the country’s mint. He changed the family name from Khadouri to Tchenguiz after moving to the UK.

Mr Tchenguiz lost hundreds of millions in the 2008 crash, including through the collapse of Iceland’s Kaupthing Bank, and was subject to an investigation by the UK’s Serious Fraud Office (SFO) as a result.

No charges were brought. The SFO later paid Mr Tchenguiz £1.5m to settle a lawsuit brought by the tycoon.

Mr Tchenguiz also owns significant stakes in Sainsbury’s and Mitchell & Butlers, the pub company that owns Toby Carvery and All Bar One.

data.title: Britain loses third-highest taxpayer to Greece
data.description:
Britain’s third-highest taxpayer has become the latest billionaire to quit the country as concerns grow about a potential tax raid under Andy Burnham.

Christopher Rokos, the hedge fund tycoon and philanthropist, is switching his residency to Greece.

He is the latest wealthy individual to leave the country after Labour scrapped the UK’s “non-dom” regime in April last year, meaning income earned abroad is now liable for tax.

Greece’s own non-dom regime allows people to pay a €100,000 (£86,000) flat tax on all foreign income for a period of up to 15 years.

Foreign residents must invest €500,000 in Greece, through property, businesses or stocks and bonds, to qualify for the non-dom regime.

Mr Rokos is one of Britain’s most prominent financiers, with his hedge fund managing more than $20bn (£15bn). He has a net worth of around $4bn, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaire Index.

The 55-year-old was listed as Britain’s third-biggest taxpayer last year, having paid £330m in 2025, according to The Sunday Times.

The taxes contributed by Mr Rokos last year is equivalent to the amount paid by 21,000 British households, based on the average family’s £15,700-a-year tax bill.

He was formerly a major donor to the Conservatives under David Cameron, to whom he gave £1.9m in the run-up to the 2015 elections.

He also made a record-breaking £190m donation to the University of Cambridge earlier this year, with the money used to open the Rokos School of Government.

As well as pursuing his philanthropic efforts, Mr Rokos is also currently spearheading a £175m renovation project on his 100-bed Wiltshire mansion.

This includes plans to build a tennis pavilion and cinema room at Tottenham House, his centuries-old Grade I-listed stately home.

Mr Rokos launched Rokos Capital Management in 2015, after leaving his job as a bond trader at rival hedge fund Brevan Howard in 2012.

He was recruited to work at Brevan Howard in the early-2000s by its founder, Alan Howard, who had been his boss at Credit Suisse, the investment bank. Mr Howard, a prominent Tory donor himself, left the UK for Switzerland last year.

Mr Rokos went on to build his fund into one of the world’s largest hedge funds through big bets on US stocks.

‘Bad news for all of us’

His decision to leave the UK, first reported by Bloomberg, comes as the worsening outlook for Britain’s economy has led to renewed speculation that John Healey, the new Chancellor, might increase taxes at his first Budget in Oct 28.

Mr Healey said he wouldn’t speculate on possible tax increases in his first major speech on Monday.

However, Mr Burnham has been warned by the Treasury that higher inflation and a possible oil shock from the conflict in the Middle East threaten a shock to Britain’s economy in the final few months of this year.

The Prime Minister refused to rule out a wealth tax before the Budget next month and has suggested the tax burden will have to rise.

He said in July that the Government may have “to ask for a little more” and that there is “some room” to raise taxes.

Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, introduced a record £26bn in new taxes, including by placing VAT on private schools.

Pat McFadden, the Work and Pensions Secretary, was asked about Mr Rokos’s impending departure on Tuesday morning.

He told the BBC: “I believe he’s a big philanthropist and a very successful person but I continue to believe that the UK is a great country to live in and a great country to found and grow a business.”

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Chris Rokos is Britain’s third-highest taxpayer. He has made huge contributions to charities and educational causes across our country. Yet another wealth and job creator leaving Britain is bad news for all of us.

“Whatever your personal finances, wealth creators leaving the UK means fewer opportunities for young people and leaves the rest of us paying more. This is what happens when a government hikes taxes. Our best and brightest are choosing where to live – and they are not choosing Labour’s Britain.”

The scrapping of Britain’s non-dom regime has since led to a string of exits from Britain by some of Britain’s richest people.

Thor Björgólfsson, an Icelandic investor, moved his tax residency from the UK to Italy last year. Italy has a flat tax of €300,000 per year on foreign income.

Guillaume Pousaz, the founder of Checkout.com, also left the UK last year, alongside Nassef Sawiri, Egypt’s second richest person, in response to the non-dom overhaul.

Representatives for Mr Rokos declined to comment.

data.title: Heathrow warns that Neets crisis is putting third runway at risk
data.description:
Heathrow risks a shortage of skilled workers to build its planned third runway because of Britain’s youth unemployment crisis, airport bosses have warned.

A lack of young people with the requisite qualifications may leave Heathrow and its contractors unable to find the 108,000 recruits needed for the £49bn scheme when construction begins in the 2030s, the airport warned on Monday.

Heathrow is aiming to deliver the runway, terminals, car parks, roads and other infrastructure by the mid-2030s, meaning many of the engineers required for the project would need to be employed and start training now.

However, a crisis in the number of young people going into work and training threatens to squeeze the supply of workers, it warned.

A Heathrow spokesman said: “The UK is facing significant skills shortages across many of the sectors that will be critical to delivering major infrastructure projects.

“Heathrow expansion has the potential to create thousands of skilled roles but unless we act now, there is a real risk that demand for workers will outstrip supply.

“Britain cannot build the infrastructure it needs without the people to build it.”

Nearly a million people aged 16 to 24 were not in employment, education or training (Neet) in the three months to June, according to the Office for National Statistics.

Almost 100,000 of them fear they will never escape that category, recent polling by YouGov suggests.

Heathrow’s warning came as official jobs figures released on Tuesday were expected to show unemployment remained at 4.9pc in the three months to July, with new figures on youth joblessness also expected.

To address the issue, the airport said it would establish a new body chaired by Lord Blunkett, a former Labour education secretary, and Robert Halfon, a former Tory skills minister, to help push more young people into work.

The so-called Heathrow Infrastructure Skills Council, established with the Trades Union Congress and Make UK, would seek “to ensure that when opportunities created by Heathrow expansion come forward, there is a skilled workforce ready to seize them”.

While the Government aims to gain planning permission for the runway by 2029, Heathrow will begin recruiting for some roles before then once a funding mechanism has been agreed with the Civil Aviation Authority.

The airport said the expansion plan – which aims to lift passenger numbers from 84 million a year to more than 140 million – will create jobs in engineering, construction, logistics and the wider supply chain in every British region, including 5,000 apprenticeships.

A spokesman added: “At a time when almost one million young people are not in education, employment or training, the council will help identify how these young people who want opportunities now can gain the skills, experience and pathways they need to access rewarding careers.”

The body plans to hold meetings with employers, colleagues and training providers across the UK on how to secure a “skills pipeline” in conjunction with mayors and local authorities.

Lord Blunkett said that if the Government is serious about tackling youth unemployment, it must continue to progress nationally significant projects like Heathrow “with absolute urgency”.

Alan Milburn, the former health secretary who is leading an independent review of young people and work, said the runway project had the potential to “make a real difference by connecting young people who need jobs to opportunities, skills and experience that can change the course of their lives”.

data.title: Burnham faces backlash over Thames Water nationalisation rethink
data.description:
Andy Burnham is facing a backlash from Labour MPs after reportedly shelving plans to place Thames Water into emergency administration.

Backbenchers have urged the Prime Minister to “hold his nerve” over proposals to put the debt-laden water company into a special administration regime, a type of nationalisation.

Mr Burnham has been a fierce critic of Thames Water and has previously said it should be nationalised. He has also frequently promised to bring Britain’s utilities under greater public control.

However, officials have raised concerns about the cost of a possible administration to the taxpayer, as well as the prospect of legal challenges from rival bidders for Thames Water.

The Government is now working on whether there is a viable alternative for putting the utility into administration, with a decision unlikely for several months, according to The Times.

The prospect of Mr Burnham putting the group into administration is looking increasingly slim, according to the report.

The Government’s apparent reticence in bringing Thames into public ownership sparked a furious response from Labour backbenchers.

Jon Trickett, the MP for Normanton and Hemsworth, said: “Privatisation of water has been a disaster. It’s a natural monopoly.

“Worse still, management has proved to be less than competent. Andy Burnham should hold his nerve and stick to his promise.”

Kim Johnson, the Labour MP for Liverpool Riverside, said: “The Prime Minister’s priorities are wrong here.

“Thames Water has been a byword for failure, underinvestment and mismanagement. If we allow it to carry on failing customers with no meaningful consequences, what message does that send?

“This summer has shown just how serious the risk of water shortages is. Public ownership cannot come quick enough.”

The Treasury could face a bill of about £2bn if Thames Water is put into special administration regime, reflecting the funding the company says it needs to remain operational until the end of next year.

Any administration would allow the firm, which supplies about 16 million customers across London and southern England, to continue providing essential services while a long-term buyer was found.

Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, also urged the Prime Minister to bring the water industry into public ownership. He said: “Privatised water has ripped us off for far too long.

“Sky-high bills. Water shortages. Polluted rivers. Sewage in the sea.

“No more hesitation, no half measures – we need water in public hands now.”

Mr Burnham’s rethink is likely to be welcomed by Thames Water’s creditors, who have been scrambling to secure control of the utility with a proposed £10bn restructuring.

The company has been struggling under a £20bn debt pile and risks running out of cash as soon as October.

Its lenders lined up four new board directors on Monday as part of a potential clear-out of its existing leadership.

The proposed new board would include Mike McTighe, the Openreach chairman, Liz Barber, the former Yorkshire Water chief executive, Clive Selley, the former Openreach chief executive and Dame Bernadette Kelly, a former permanent secretary at the Department for Transport.

Under a 10-year turnaround plan, the new investors said they would take no dividends for a decade or until Thames Water returned to the stock market with a London listing.

Thames Water’s ageing network has been under renewed pressure from one of the driest summers on record.

It has been battling more than 1,000 leaks every week as the clay soil in the ground dries out and causes pipes to crack.

A government source insisted that all options were on the table amid talks with creditors.

data.title: Developer turns back on housing to chase data centre rush
data.description:
A leading property developer is quitting the housing market to cash in on soaring demand for data centres.

Land development group Harworth said it would cease work on residential sites “entirely” because data centre projects and warehouses are more profitable.

The FTSE 250 business, which regenerates brownfield land for new property developments, said it would “exit the residential sector entirely and accelerate the reallocation of capital to higher-returning opportunities”. These include data centres, logistics and industrial projects.

Labour has pledged to build 1.5 million homes to help tackle Britain’s housing crisis. It has also sought to speed up data centre construction to turn the country into an AI power.

But Harworth’s move suggests the two ambitions are at odds. Although Britain needs more homes, AI projects are proving more lucrative for investors.

The value of Harworth’s land portfolio for housing fell by £16.9m in the first half of the year, which was blamed on challenging market conditions and persistently high build costs for housebuilders.

Harworth said housebuilders were grappling with “rising construction costs, additional policy costs, higher taxes, and a growing array of levies” that had “collectively eroded the viability of many new developments”.

In contrast, its industrial portfolio had produced an average annual return of 24.5pc over the past five years, compared with lower returns from housing.

Angela Rayner, the Housing Secretary, has ushered in planning reforms, including measures to make it easier to build homes and data centres on brownfield land.

Nonetheless, Britain still needs to build more than 1,000 new homes a day to meet Labour’s housing goals, according to Land Value Calculator’s monitor, double its current pace of 547 a day.

Harworth said it was progressing a sale of land for a data centre in Leeds to Microsoft and was in advanced talks to sell a plot for a second major data centre. Four more sites for so-called “hyperscale” data centres have also been identified.

It said its existing data centre portfolio could generate £293m of profit for the business.

The Government has designated data centres as “critical national infrastructure” and has created AI growth zones across the country to boost their construction.

Harworth is battling a takeover attempt from John Whittaker, a Manchester billionaire, who owns a 30pc stake in the business through his company Peel Group.

Harworth rebuffed his latest £583m offer on Wednesday and said it was “unequivocal in its rejection”.

data.title: Drivers to miss out on car finance payouts after lender’s takeover
data.description:
Drivers will miss out on motor finance payouts after a lender was rescued from collapse by one of its largest funders.

Blue Motor Finance collapsed into administration this year after facing a £50m bill for redress claims related to the mis-selling of motor finance.

The business was salvaged in a pre-pack administration at the end of July by Hodge Bank. However, as part of the deal, Hodge Bank will not take on the redress claims.

It means many drivers will end up at the back of the queue among the failed lender’s other creditors, missing out on the full amount of compensation they would have otherwise been entitled to.

Hodge Bank was one of Blue Motor Finance’s largest funders, providing a £540m funding facility in 2023. It is understood that none of the bank’s funding contributed directly to motor finance claims that fell afoul of the City watchdog.

Cabot Square, which owned Blue Motor Finance until it collapsed, was contacted for comment. According to Cabot Square’s website, Blue Motor Finance was “one of the UK’s premier consumer motor finance companies, lending over £1bn to over 120,000 customers”.

MPs have called on the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), which approved the Blue Motor Finance rescue deal, to reconsider, given the implications for motorists who were mis-sold car finance.

Bobby Dean, a Liberal Democrat MP on Treasury select committee, said the deal amounted to a “get-out-of-jail-free card”.

He said: “It is disgraceful to learn of firms exploiting legal loopholes to avoid their responsibilities. Using administration as a backdoor to strip out compensation claims while holding on to the profitable parts of the business sets a dangerous precedent.

“The FCA should be protecting consumers who were ripped off. It is disgraceful that they are giving firms a get-out-of-jail free card in this way.”

Blue Motor Finance had been loss-making for years before the redress scheme tipped it over the edge.

According to administration documents, the company had only provisioned around £10m for redress payments by October last year, based on the fact that it was challenging the FCA’s scheme.

This was despite the lender estimating that in a worst-case scenario it could face liabilities between £50m and £70m.

An FCA spokesman said: “We recognise Blue Motor’s customers will be disappointed they’re unlikely to receive all the compensation they’re owed. Blue Motor had been in serious financial difficulties for some time. Without this deal, it was much less likely any compensation would be paid.

“Lenders and their directors are responsible for ensuring they can meet their financial responsibilities. We would take a very dim view of any that tried to shirk them.”

Hodge Bank declined to comment but Richard Saulet, its chief executive, said at the time of the rescue deal that it had protected jobs and was the best outcome for redress claimants.

“By acquiring the business through the pre-pack process, we have been able to secure continuity of operations, protect jobs and ensure that customers continue to be supported,” Mr Saulet said.

“Importantly, this structure also maximises the value available to be distributed to redress claimants, delivering a better outcome than would otherwise have been possible.”

data.title: Amazon admits selling fake ‘net zero’ plugs to UK shoppers
data.description:
Amazon is still selling dangerous fake “energy saving” plugs that pose a potential fire risk, despite telling MPs it would take the listings down.

The scam plug-in products claim to cut electricity bills by up to 30pc by “stabilising” voltage and “balancing” electric current to “optimise” the performance of household appliances.

But tests on eight devices carried out by consumer group Which? found no evidence that any of the claims were justified and concluded that all were illegal to sell in the UK and posed a serious safety risk.

The hazard was raised by Joshua Reynolds, the Liberal Democrat MP for Maidenhead, at a hearing of the business and trade select committee in June.

The MP asked senior executives at online retailers Amazon and eBay: “How is it possible to buy products that you know are completely fake and a fire risk?”

Thomas Bell, the UK lead for product safety and external relations at Amazon, told the committee that Amazon would order an internal investigation.

He said at the time: “We have controls in place to prevent listings where the claims are not substantiated ... These two items appear to have slipped through that net.”

Monica Ariño, the US tech giant’s director for public policy, has now written to the committee admitting that a “technical issue in our automated classification system” had prevented the devices being “proactively detected” by its filters.

She said: “The products identified have been removed from sale, and we have also conducted a comprehensive audit across multiple European marketplace.”

However, The Telegraph has found that it is still possible to buy the devices at Amazon.co.uk despite the retailer’s pledge to act.

Mr Reynolds said he will be writing to Amazon bosses to demand an explanation of how plugs could still be on sale.

He said: “Amazon has got some proper questions they have to answer. These are exactly the same products tested by Which?. Not only are the sellers still able to list these on the website, but they are sponsored ads so they are paying Amazon to put them at the top of the page.”

The devices were typically priced at less than £10 and marketed themselves as an “eco plug” or an “energy-saving box”. Some claimed to cut household bills by up to a third, playing on consumers’ fears about rising energy bills and reducing their carbon emissions.

The products were being sold by AliExpress, eBay, Shein, Temu and TikTok Shop as well as Amazon.

More than half had pins that were too small, not straight or could easily break off in the socket.

One device available on Amazon with more than a dozen one-star ratings lacked a fuse or any other protection. One reviewer warned: “The only thing these boxes will achieve is a house fire.”

Sue Davies, head of consumer protection policy at Which?, said: “One quick search for ‘energy saving plug’ is all Which? researchers needed to find more than a dozen examples of these dangerous products. In light of this, Amazon’s letter to the select committee comes across as little more than PR damage control.

“Which? has reported this unsafe product to Amazon several times over the years, but this is just the latest in a long list of examples why we don’t believe Amazon and other online marketplaces will take meaningful action until they are compelled by law.”

Amazon was contacted for comment.

data.title: Billionaire Brexiteer Crispin Odey’s fall from grace
data.description:
Stooped about the witness box, Crispin Odey was barely audible as he was cross-examined by a lawyer for the City watchdog.

The normally ebullient hedge fund boss, 67, was giving evidence as part of his attempt to overturn a lifetime ban from the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).

The hearing earlier this year focused on an arcane section of the watchdog’s rule book: whether Odey – who twice fired his executive committee before it could discipline him about allegations he “lacked integrity” – acted “recklessly” and breached its rules.

But everyone in the room knew the subtext to the proceedings: the hedge fund tycoon’s history of alleged sexual misconduct stretching back decades.

Perhaps it was the toxicity of these allegations that made Odey vacillate between proud and evasive when answering questions from the FCA’s chief counsel, Clare Sibson KC.

Asked later by the judge why he chose to close Odey Asset Management (OAM), his eponymous hedge fund, instead of trying to sell his stake, he responded: “I am a proud man.”

This defiance pushed Odey into an expensive legal battle with the City watchdog – one which cast fresh light on repeated allegations of sexual misconduct stretching back decades.

That battle ended in defeat for Odey on Monday. A court upheld a £1.53m fine for the financier – reduced from an initial claim of £1.8m – and a lifetime ban from financial services, ruling in favour of the City watchdog.

The Upper Tribunal, which decides on appeals against the FCA, ruled in its favour, finding Odey had deliberately worked to frustrate an internal investigation into misconduct allegations, while showing “reckless disregard” for City rules.

It said Odey had “repeatedly prioritised his own interests at the expense of risk of detriment to OAM, its staff members and investors” while seeing “nothing wrong with his approach”.

“Mr Odey’s only purpose was self-preservation and to avoid being held to account for his behaviour,” the FCA said.

For many observers, the spectacle of Odey in court laid bare the other side of a man once lauded as one of the “sharpest and most contrarian brains” in the City.

Who is Crispin Odey?

Odey was a rarity among his secretive hedge fund peers, enjoying an outsized and flamboyant public persona.

Born to Yorkshire industrialists, Odey was educated at Harrow and Christ Church, Oxford, where he read history and economics.

After graduating, Odey was handed control of the 4,000-acre Hotham Hall estate that had been in his family for centuries, but was soon forced to sell everything off to settle his father’s substantial debts.

After entering the City, he was briefly married to Rupert Murdoch’s eldest daughter, Prudence, but the relationship only lasted 15 months before they divorced.

Then, in 1991, he married Nichola Pease, a fund manager whose family helped found Barclays, creating a power couple often called the “Posh and Becks” of the City. The same year, Odey set up his eponymous firm, with backing from early investors, including George Soros.

During the ensuing decades, Odey became one of London’s best-known hedge fund tycoons, in part because of his astute ability to cash in on chaos.

The hedge fund boss correctly predicted that the value of insurance companies would rise in the wake of 9/11, before pocketing £28m in 2008 after successfully predicting the financial crisis.

The Brexit-backing financier gained further notoriety among political opponents in 2016 when he made £220m by betting that markets would drop after the referendum result.

“Il mattino ha l’oro in bocca [The morning has gold in its mouth],” Odey said to the BBC on the morning after the vote.

Odey has not been immune to failure. OAM, whose assets under management stood at $13.3bn (£9.8bn) at its peak in 2015, went through volatile shifts in fortune. One of his funds lost 44pc of its value in 19914.

Undoubtedly, though, Odey has done well out of his bets. His pay peaked at £36m in 2010 and he and his wife were estimated to be worth £775m in 2019.

In addition to his own fund, Odey held a significant stake in Sky, which he cashed in after its $39bn takeover by Comcast.

Odey, who in 2010 threatened to leave the UK in protest against high tax rates, has complemented his financial gains with forays into politics. He made political donations valued at £1.7m between 2007 and 2019.

Some went to Boris Johnson and the Conservative Party. More recently he donated to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. The majority of his donations were channelled into groups campaigning for Brexit.

Odey also captured the imagination with his wholehearted embrace of the rarefied world of Mayfair high finance.

At more than 6ft tall and of ample build, Odey strikes an imposing figure.

Known for his trademark City uniform of red braces, the financier has also been described as a “country gent”, whose passion for enriching himself was rivalled only by his enthusiasm for country pursuits, such as hunting and fishing.

Nor has he shied away from displays of extravagance. He spent more than £130,000 building a Palladian-style chicken coop in 2012, nicknamed “Cluckingham Palace” by the tabloids, at his Gloucestershire estate, Eastbach Court.

The financier, who has a sausage named after him, was also notorious for his prodigious appetite. At one midweek meal with a journalist, he paired steak and kidney pudding and mash with a “side order” of a loin of beef and two bottles of wine.

Odey’s larger-than-life personality contrasted with allegations of a more menacing side. Media reporting and the lengthy dispute with the City watchdog have detailed incidents in which women were allegedly sexually assaulted. In one case, a woman accused him of rape, which he strenuously denied.

His reputation earned him the nickname “the octopus”.

The allegations first emerged publicly in 2020, when Odey was charged with indecent assault on a woman in 1998 after she accused him of groping her in his Chelsea home.

The trial, which came in the wake of the “Me Too” movement, gained significant publicity, with the hedge fund chief pictured leaving court clad in a mask and flanked by his wife.

Odey admitted propositioning the woman, then 26, but denied assault. He was acquitted in 2021, with the judge ruling there were “inconsistencies” in the woman’s account.

Two years later, Tortoise, and then the Financial Times, published investigations outlining allegations that Odey sexually harassed or assaulted 13 women during the course of 25 years.

Odey settled civil claims from five women in May, weeks before they were to be heard in court.

The lawsuits include allegations that Mr Odey raped a woman in the mid-1990s, an accusation he called “wholly false”.

Odey also mounted a £79m defamation claim against the Financial Times, but dropped it in April.

The consequences have already rippled through Odey’s private life. He and Pease, who have three children together, divorced soon after his court case in 2021. Odey has since remarried Diana Vitkova, a Bulgarian-born finance executive 26 years his junior.

Meanwhile, OAM collapsed in 2023 as major banks cut ties and investors pulled their money, forcing the company to start winding down its funds.

‘Playing the victim’

Odey mounted his challenge against the FCA ruling earlier this year, seemingly in an attempt to cling on to what might have remained of his status within the industry.

Yet the hearings in the Upper Tribunal did little to repair his reputation, particularly after he failed to have the sexual harassment claims excluded from the case.

By the end of the hearings, the FCA’s lawyers had accused Odey of submitting “false evidence” to the court and a “brazen” attempt to create a “false history” of events.

“Mr Odey displayed a remarkable absence of self-awareness, was evasive, inconsistent, and had a tendency to attack others whilst playing the victim,” the regulator argued in submissions to the court.

Witness statements and court testimony paint a picture of a working environment controlled by a domineering and at times abusive boss.

Odey Asset Management, which was based in a five-storey Georgian townhouse in Mayfair, operated much like a feudal state, with Odey, controlling 75pc of the fund. He had a reputation for reportedly hiring “earls and girls”, with a predominantly male and former public-school workforce and women hired usually only as receptionists.

The court heard claims that OAM was an “old boys’ club”, with documents suggesting that executives at the firm had “very similar backgrounds” to Mr Odey.

For a string of women at the firm, however, it went far further than a gender imbalance.

OAM commissioned law firm Simmons & Simmons to carry out an investigation in 2020 into its founder’s conduct. The resulting report detailed at least 46 misconduct claims against Odey dating back to 2003.

The court heard one incident in which it was claimed Odey gave a female employee a massage before “groping her breasts”. He was then accused of trying to manipulate the woman “into silence”. The hedge fund boss has blamed his actions on a dental sedative he took earlier that day.

Yet this incident was described as part of a culture of “prolific sexual harassment” that was “accepted as part of the deal” of working at OAM. As one of his former employees testified, Odey was a “sex pest” who found it “hard to control himself” around women.

On the stand, Odey acknowledged staff thought he was a “creepy old man” but defended his behaviour with female subordinates. “Maybe I am a dinosaur; I cannot see how any of that can be sexual harassment,” he said.

Odey argued that the FCA was under “political pressure” and “sought a totemic case”, adding that the watchdog had a “pre-determined view of his fitness and propriety”.

That the allegations took so long to surface has in part been put down to a culture of complicity within OAM. But it was also a result of Odey’s concerted efforts to bury the allegations and oust anyone who threatened to make them public.

‘Evidence of gross misconduct’

After the damning internal report was published in 2021, OAM’s executive committee issued a final written warning to Odey regarding his behaviour. The court heard that it cut Odey’s pay by 40pc, after pressure from the FCA.

It also banned him from physical contact with other staff members, excluding handshaking, and inviting or accompanying any female members of staff to events or shopping trips or contacting them by text or email.

That summer a new allegation surfaced after Odey told a temporary receptionist she should “take a lover”, the court heard, and then accidentally showed her an indecent photo of his girlfriend while sharing pictures from a fishing trip.

The executive committee scheduled a disciplinary hearing in November to consider whether Odey had breached its final warning. But Odey acted first. On Christmas Eve, the tycoon sacked the entire committee – a move described by one witness as the “nuclear option”.

Odey subsequently decided that the disciplinary hearing into his conduct would be indefinitely postponed. He appointed new committee members, but after disagreement about how to proceed with the hearing, he sacked this board as well.

Some of Odey’s former employees tell a story of bullying. In his witness statement, Thomas Richards, OAM’s former chief operating officer and a member of the committee, said the hedge fund boss had called him “f-----g spineless” and threatened to shut down the fund.

Another executive said he felt “physically threatened” by Odey after recommending he work from home or take a sabbatical. Jack Satt, the firm’s compliance chief who resigned in the wake of the scandal, said Odey offered him £1m and a future role as chief executive if he stayed on.

These executives were not beyond reproach. Howard Cornwell, a former FCA official, described the outcome of the initial disciplinary hearing as “unsatisfactory”, saying he believed there was “evidence of gross misconduct which would normally lead to dismissal”.

He said: “Supervision was of the view that OAM’s decision in not removing Mr Odey, as controller and founder of OAM, was motivated in part by self-interest given the potential impact of removing Mr Odey on the firm as a whole.”

But there was no doubting Odey was a force to be reckoned with. The hedge fund tycoon even took an aggressive approach towards the FCA itself, at one point threatening to “go straight to the f-----g press”.

In an explosive outburst to one official at the watchdog, he said: “You will not get away with this – I have an agreement then you little guys, trying to do your work in the shadows ... You are about to create a crisis.”

For now, the City watchdog triumphed. The tribunal ruled against Odey, upholding all five of the FCA’s allegations against the hedge fund manager, including that he threatened the watchdog’s staff.

He has two weeks to file a further appeal.

Instead of restoring his reputation, Odey’s appeals have only caused a deluge of allegations to resurface.

Therese Chambers, the FCA’s executive director of enforcement, said: “During the hearing he reinvented history, painted himself as a victim and displayed no contrition.

“That arrogant entitlement and the resulting complete disregard for proper governance means Mr Odey is unfit to work in financial services.”

And, despite Odey’s claims to the contrary, it is a crisis entirely of his own making.

data.title: London gains largest factory since Second World War
data.description:
A British start-up has opened London’s biggest factory since the Second World War as rearmament creates new work for defence manufacturers.

Isembard said the 160,000-square-foot facility would use cutting-edge technology to make components for major customers, including Babcock, Anduril and Tekever.

The company specialises in making high-precision metal components for defence equipment, including drones, military aircraft and robotic systems.

The factory in Southwark is expected to employ around 200 workers by the end of 2027 and will also serve as Isembard’s global headquarters as it expands abroad.

The opening is a boost to Andy Burnham’s push to “reindustrialise” Britain at a time when the Government is also seeking to rebuild the defence industrial base.

Higher defence spending across Europe is spurring demand for new weapons, ammunition and vehicles as the Nato alliance seeks to deter a war with Russia.

Alexander Fitzgerald, Isembard’s founder, said: “Manufacturing is the origin of our security, prosperity and sense of purpose as nations.

“No one has opened a factory like this in London since the Second World War and that tells you how far our industrial base has been allowed to shrink.”

He added: “Bringing production back onshore is the work of the next decade. What we need now are the brightest engineering minds of our generation to join us.”

‘Erosion of industrial capacity’

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, welcomed the announcement, adding: “This is exactly what reindustrialising Britain is all about. Bringing manufacturing back into the UK, backing our critical industries and creating highly skilled jobs across the country.

“It is my mission to create the conditions that businesses need to invest and expand in the UK, to drive growth and opportunity in every postcode.

“This exciting news from Isembard marks a huge vote of confidence in that ambition.”

Isembard was founded in 2025 by Mr Fitzgerald, an Army reservist and former telecoms entrepreneur, to help support Western rearmament.

According to Isembard, small businesses including family-run machine shops currently account for 95pc of component manufacturing, but are “rapidly disappearing” with the average owner being 65 years old or above – and two fifths planning to retire within five years.

“This erosion of industrial capacity is colliding with surging demand from aerospace, defence, energy and robotics companies driven by re-shoring and rising spending on critical industries,” the company said.

But using a combination of in-house software and modern factory machines, Mr Fitzgerald has argued that the British company can step in to fill this gap and even produce advanced components more cheaply than its rivals in China.

Isembard runs its own factories but also a franchised network of factories that all use its proprietary MasonOS software.

The company has gone from four sites at the start of last year to 16 as of Monday, including new factories in France and Germany.

It is targeting 100 in the UK alone by the end of 2028, an expansion that it says will create 2,200 highly-skilled jobs.

Isambard’s new base in Southwark is close to where Isambard Kingdom Brunel – the engineer who inspired the company’s differently spelt name — spent his early career digging the Thames Tunnel out from Rotherhithe.

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: Guardian staff threaten walkout over pay as paper hails record revenues
data.description:
Guardian staff have threatened to walk out in a row over pay as the newspaper hailed its highest-ever revenues.

The National Union of Journalists (NUJ) is to hold an indicative ballot of members over whether to strike in protest against the company’s latest pay offer.

Union bosses said the move followed a “sustained lack of progress” in pay discussions, branding the latest offer “inadequate”.

Staff are in revolt about a proposal to increase salaries by 3.85pc. While the uplift is above inflation, the union said it did not “meaningfully” address cost of living pressures.

Journalists have also complained about increased workloads under editor Katharine Viner’s Project Berger strategy, which includes greater focus on audio and video and expansion in the US and Australia.

On Thursday, The Guardian revealed revenues grew to £282m in its latest financial year, up 2pc and a record for the media group’s news operations.

The newspaper, which does not charge for online subscriptions but asks readers to make one-off or monthly contributions, reported a 17pc increase in reader revenues to £126m last year.

Revenue generated outside the UK rose 8pc to £115m, suggesting the company’s international push is starting to pay off.

Bosses said growth was particularly strong in the US, where the paper now has more than half a million paying readers.

Despite rising revenues, The Guardian, which is owned by the £1.2bn Scott Trust endowment, lost £17m last year, though this narrowed from £24m the previous year.

The newspaper’s resilient performance is likely to further fuel anger among journalists who argue it could afford a more generous pay deal.

The strike ballot, which is open until next Wednesday, is indicative, meaning the union will not be committed to industrial action in the event of a yes vote.

Nevertheless, it underscores the level of discontent at the publisher. The two sides are entering an Acas mediation process.

Restructuring

The prospect of fresh strike action will create a headache for Guardian bosses two years after staff staged a 48-hour walkout in protest against the sale of The Observer to news start-up Tortoise, led by James Harding, the former BBC News boss.

The sale of the Sunday title went ahead despite the strike, and the Scott Trust invested £5m in Tortoise as part of the deal.

However, it opted not to participate in Tortoise’s latest funding round, which closed last month.

The Guardian has separately outlined proposals to stop using “casual” workers and instead create up to 95 new roles.

However, some staff have raised concerns that the newspaper is preparing to employ an army of low-paid young graduates, similar to the model employed by struggling publisher Reach.

A Guardian spokesman said: “Negotiations are ongoing, and we believe we have offered a fair pay increase which is above inflation and compares very favourably with other employers in our sector.

“We are reviewing how we engage with and manage casuals in editorial to ensure the system is better suited to their needs and our operational requirements. We are engaging constructively with the NUJ as we undertake this work.”

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: Labour’s wealth raid ‘kills off ultra-luxury homes in London’
data.description:
Labour’s wealth tax raid combined with stringent planning laws has effectively killed off ultra-luxury property developments in London, experts have warned.

Branded residences – luxury homes with hotel services – are often viewed as symbols of status and wealth creation.

Some of the UK’s best-known examples include the Mandarin Oriental at One Hyde Park, and the OWO Residences by Raffles in Mayfair.

But a combination of recent planning rules restricting flat sizes, weak demand and Labour’s hostility towards the super-rich has prevented property developers from building them in Britain.

It means a 120-home project in St John’s Wood, scheduled to finish in 2028, is likely to be the last of its kind according to a new report from property consultancy Knight Frank.

Gareth Stow, the chief executive of St John’s Wood Square, said in the report: “It’s probably the last super-prime scheme in London of any scale.”

Planning rules adopted by Westminster city council in 2021 introduced a 200 sq m size limit on new homes, covering neighbourhoods including Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge.

St John’s Wood Square secured planning consent in 2015, making it the last development of its size that will deliver flats averaging 300 sq m.

But at the same time, wealthy buyers have been scared off by Labour’s tax crackdown on the super-rich.

A number of billionaires have left Britain in protest against higher taxes on investments, inheritance and capital gains, as well as the abolition of non-dom status.

The latest to flee is Chris Rokos, the hedge fund billionaire, who is preparing to move his residency to Greece amid concerns Labour will raise taxes in the upcoming Budget.

“A realignment of capital is under way at the top end of the market,” says Rupert des Forges of Knight Frank.

“A lot of these buyers have reduced what they are going to spend here because of the cost of purchasing and sentiment towards wealth. Everybody is a lot more transient than they used to be.”

The UK’s hostility towards the super-rich has stood in stark contrast to countries such as Italy and Greece, which have instead introduced policies designed to attract more wealthy overseas buyers.

The drop-off in construction has meant that London’s market for branded residences has been outpaced by Dubai, the US and Thailand.

The global market has tripled in a decade, rising from 354 schemes in 2015 to 903 at the end of 2025. The number of projects will exceed 1,000 this year.

The report also shows there is growing buyer appetite for concepts such as longevity clinics, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, cryotherapy, sound-healing studios and other “biohacking-focused” wellness facilities.

A government spokesperson said: “Property markets are influenced by a range of factors, and SDLT forecasts are produced independently by the OBR.

“We are getting on with the job of building the homes this country needs, such as through our Social and Affordable Homes Programme, driving the biggest council housebuilding revival in decades.”

data.title: Trump attacks ‘sick conspiracy’ against AI
data.description:
Donald Trump has attacked what he calls a “sick conspiracy” against AI after the head of Anthropic called for a slowdown in the technology’s development.

The US president warned that China would benefit after the bosses of Silicon Valley’s top AI companies backed calls to restrict AI development for safety reasons, calling the concerns a “hoax”.

He also launched a tirade against Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, whom he accused of trying to be a “perfect little angel”.

Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social: “The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel’ – and we will continue to do so!

“We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”

Mr Amodei released a letter at the weekend calling for an industry-wide slowdown, endorsed by the US government, to prevent safety issues going “seriously wrong”.

In response, Mr Trump wrote: “Concerning AI, when, in the history of business, did anyone see the leaders of an industry call for regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy.

“AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.”

JD Vance, the US vice-president, echoed Mr Trump’s comments, calling tech leaders’ requests a “Trojan horse”.

He added: “I have to say, just personally, I feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them.

“It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse.”

OpenAI has since called on the UK Government to introduce mandatory safety rules for major AI developers.

Under proposals supported by the company, the UK’s AI Security Institute would play a central role in third-party testing and creating adaptive technical standards.

Tom Duff-Gordon, the company’s head of policy in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, told Politico: “OpenAI is in a position to support legislation in the UK to establish durable, mandatory, capability-based requirements for frontier AI that would build on the set of voluntary commitments that we currently have.”

Under the plans, Britain would move from the current system of voluntary agreements with AI companies to enforceable standards, bringing the UK in line with emerging frameworks in the EU and US.

The Government has not yet put forward plans for AI safety legislation, despite pressure from backbench MPs.

US tech stocks fell sharply on Wall Street after AI bosses called for a slowdown, with the Nasdaq Composite dropping by as much as 1.3pc.

Nvidia, the world’s largest listed company and a manufacturer of semiconductors used in the AI race, plunged by 4.2pc while fellow chipmaker AMD dropped 6.2pc.

The main European indexes in France, Germany and Spain were all down sharply on Monday after falls in South Korea and Japan overnight.

data.title: Wind farms accused of pushing up bills by exploiting loophole
data.description:
Wind farm owners have been accused of pushing up household bills by exploiting a “loophole” in green energy subsidies.

The loophole involves contracts for difference (CfDs), the 15- or 20-year fixed-price deals that are handed to wind farms to give developers certainty about their future income.

These are used to underpin the finances of most renewable energy schemes and are ultimately funded through consumer bills.

Ministers have repeatedly described CfDs as good value because they lock in relatively low-priced supplies of power for consumers that can shield them from price increases during crises.

But some developers have repeatedly exploited a rule allowing them to delay the start of their contracts so they can sell power at higher market rates instead. This has allowed some to reap huge windfalls.

Ministers closed the loophole in 2023, but projects awarded CfDs before then can still use it.

One energy executive claimed the situation was an “absolute p---take”.

They accused some developers of “making out like bandits” from the arrangement at the expense of millions of households and businesses, at a time when the US-Iran war has sent power prices surging.

One wind farm, Seagreen, off the coast of Angus, Scotland, is thought to have made about £27m extra by exploiting the loophole in the past two years, according to an analysis of market data by The Telegraph.

The scheme’s first phase secured a CfD in 2019 and construction finished in 2023.

Its CfD had a target start date of March 2025, but this has been repeatedly pushed back, with owners SSE, TotalEnergies and PTTEP now saying that they expect to activate it in March 2027.

There is no suggestion of wrongdoing by the companies, which must activate the CfD by a “hard stop” deadline of September 2028.

Spot power prices in Britain have jumped about £75 per megawatt-hour (MWh) during 2026 and are currently sitting at around £156 per MWh.

This means a wind farm, such as Seagreen, which was awarded a fixed CfD price of about £55 per MWh in today’s prices, can currently reap substantial profits by selling electricity at market rates.

David Turver, an independent energy analyst, argued this went against the spirit of CfDs, which are meant to help support the business cases of wind farms.

He said: “The ability to delay the start of CfDs was originally intended to help developers manage the risk of construction delays.

“But in some cases, the wind farms have been built already and they are simply choosing not to activate the contracts so they can get higher merchant power prices. They are benefitting in that way from higher gas prices.”

The energy executive added: “The CfD bid they made was predicated on what they [would] earn over the period covering construction, plus operations, plus the cost of capital – so the extra earnings now are pure windfall.

“In these times of high energy prices, they make out like bandits before activating it at their discretion.”

The Government previously urged wind farms to “act fairly on this matter, recognising the public support they have received for development”, before closing the loophole in 2023.

A spokesman for Seagreen Wind Energy Limited said on Friday: “In August 2026, we updated the Low Carbon Contracts Company regarding the expected start date for the CfD for Seagreen Phase 1.

“This has been done in accordance with the terms and conditions of the contract.”

data.title: Channel 4 to axe 300 jobs in biggest ever round of cuts
data.description:
Channel 4 is expected to cut around a quarter of its workforce in the biggest redundancy round in its four-decade history.

Priya Dogra, the broadcaster’s new chief executive, is expected to confirm the cuts as part of a broader strategy on Wednesday at an all-staff meeting.

Channel 4 is still finalising numbers, but the cuts will affect between 300 and 325 roles, The Guardian reported. A spokesman declined to comment, saying staff would be informed of the measures first.

Layoffs of that scale would represent about 25pc of the broadcaster’s workforce, which stood at 1,276 last year. It would mark the deepest cuts in the history of Channel 4, which was founded under Margaret Thatcher in 1982. It last announced 240 job losses two years ago.

The youth-focused broadcaster is attempting to shore up its finances as it undertakes a difficult shift to the digital era.

It has faced an exodus of younger viewers to streaming and social media rivals such as Netflix and YouTube and has struggled to reverse a decline in ad revenues from traditional TV.

The company fell into a £10m deficit last year – its third consecutive year in the red – though losses narrowed.

Ms Dogra, who replaced Alex Mahon as chief executive in March, has been reviewing Channel 4’s structure and strategy.

The company, which is publicly owned but commercially funded, secured permission from the Government this summer to access the remaining half of a £150m debt facility to ease its financial pressure.

It is unclear which roles will be affected by the latest cuts, but London could face significant losses, as the broadcaster has outlined plans to sell and move out of its Westminster offices.

Bosses have also pledged to increase jobs in the nations and regions after opening a new headquarters in Leeds.

Ms Dogra could also seek to shake up Channel 4’s commissioning strategy to win back audiences. The broadcaster has been spending less on new programming in recent years to keep a lid on costs.

Ian Katz, Channel 4’s head of programmes, will step down next month after nearly nine years in the role.

Mr Katz, the group’s longest-serving content chief, is credited with discovering shows such as Taskmaster. However, Channel 4 has faced criticism for being too reliant on old hits, such as Gogglebox and The Great British Bake Off.

Jonathan Allan, Channel 4’s former chief operating officer, who was in the running for the top job, also stepped down this year.

A Channel 4 spokesman said: “As we have shared publicly, under the leadership of our new CEO, we have been assessing Channel 4’s strategic direction, including a comprehensive review of the structure, shape and size of our organisation.

“We have committed to keeping Channel 4 staff updated in a timely and transparent way, so any organisational change will be shared with them first, and we won’t be commenting on speculation.”

data.title: Sewage dumped into rivers as rain overwhelms water system
data.description:
Water companies are pumping sewage into rivers as ageing wastewater systems struggle to cope with the return of rain.

Campaign group River Action said there had been 4,600 sewage spill incidents across England and Scotland in the past 48 hours as storm overflows were overwhelmed.

Sewage has been flowing into the River Derwent in Derbyshire for 15 hours, while a spill into the River Windrush in Oxfordshire has been ongoing for 13 hours.

In the UK, a sewage spill is considered legal if it happens during exceptionally heavy rain and only if the sewage is discharged through an outlet named in the water company’s permit.

The incidents in recent days follow the return of rain after weeks of drought, with thunderstorms forecast across England during the bank holiday weekend.

However, Feargal Sharkey, the musician-turned-rivers campaigner, said the level of sewage seeping into the country’s rivers reflected the poor state of Britain’s water system rather than the weather.

Mr Sharkey said: “When there’s the merest hint of rain, copious amounts of sewage are dumped into our rivers and into the water around our beaches. Yet again the profiteering and failure of our water companies to invest is exposed.”

Thames Water spilt effluent into rivers for more than 100,000 hours in 2025, despite it being a dry year.

Severn Trent Water was the only water company to receive a top rating for its environmental performance last year, but nonetheless recorded more than 30,000 spillage incidents.

Utility companies are in the middle of an investment programme meant to reduce sewage spills. Water UK, which represents Britain’s water companies, said the industry was “tripling investment over the next five years to halve spills from storm overflows and upgrade the capacity of 1,700 wastewater treatment works”.

However, Mark Lloyd, the chief executive of River Action UK, said the investment was too little, too late.

“It is disgraceful that funding for new infrastructure to prevent sewage overflows – and for maintenance of existing assets – was restricted over the past 20 years,” he said.

Mr Lloyd added that the recent spillages were particularly bad, as the preceding drought meant the sewage was potentially more environmentally damaging.

He told The Telegraph: “Sewage overflows after long dry periods can be particularly damaging because there can be accumulations of concentrated sewage in the network that get flushed out into rivers that have low flows and oxygen levels, greatly increasing the impact on fish, invertebrates and other wildlife.”

Andy Burnham has pledged to assert greater control of water companies, saying this month that he was “angry” about the industry’s performance, including on pollution.
