data.title: Stop clutching your pearls over state capitalism. It never went away
data.description:
The reaction of Right-wing pundits to the US government’s extraordinary intervention in Venezuelan oil has been predictably alarmist. But it shouldn’t be.

Far from signalling the end of capitalism or democracy, it’s the clearest sign yet that the West is finally prepared to do whatever it takes to protect the free world from authoritarian rivals that have learned to exploit its openness against it.

Under the emerging arrangement, the Pentagon – acting through the Biden-created Office of Strategic Capital (OSC) – is taking a direct stake in a venture controlling huge Venezuelan oil concessions to encourage American companies back into the country.

That may sound strikingly conflicting given the free-market norms that have governed the West’s economic order since the Reagan and Thatcher era.

But dig deeper, and one realises that the laissez-faire system we thought we had may never have been quite as entrenched as we thought.

To a lesser or greater degree, the influence of the state has always been present in commerce and markets, particularly when vital national interests are at stake.

Nick Butler, Gordon Brown’s former energy adviser who once managed BP’s relationship with the British government, provided a telling example of this fact on a panel about the rise of state capitalism at a finance festival earlier this year. He recalled how Tony Blair had one day summoned him to No 10 to advise that BP should invest in Russia as a matter of government policy. BP duly did.

For Butler, therefore, there is nothing particularly surprising about the US government becoming increasingly interventionist in trade, commerce or markets. “I think it is entirely natural,” he told the audience.

“There is a mutual relationship of mutual benefit between the two. It may not always be as transparent as it should be, but I think it’s there.”

He reiterated the point to me this week. “Energy is too important for governments to leave to the free market because it represents such an important part of economic life and therefore of national security,” he said.

Seen in this light, the national-security apparatus has always reserved the right to override the normal conventions of liberal government when vital interests are threatened. This includes on a contingency basis, as is happening now.

What is changing, therefore, is not the relationship itself but its visibility: what was previously implicit, and often conducted behind closed doors, is essentially becoming explicit as national security threats deepen.

Nor is this merely an American phenomenon. Andy Burnham this week signalled that Britain too will move towards greater public control of essential services to protect its sovereign capacity in strategic sectors including energy, steel and defence.

For those on the Right, the knee-jerk reaction, quite understandably, is to assume the worst: a Left-wing government is predictably indulging in the opportunity to over-extend itself into areas it has no business in.

Such an assumption may even have been fair historically. In the current context, however, it potentially misses the bigger picture. When sovereignty comes under threat, the interests of those seeking more government control increasingly align – at least temporarily – with those who prefer a freer system. In political theory, this is known as “the state of exception”.

We did not, after all, triumph in either World War under a free-market system.

In 1914, Winston Churchill, then the first lord of the admiralty, persuaded the government to buy a controlling stake in the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, BP’s predecessor, to secure fuel supplies for the Royal Navy. Moreover, the British government only disposed of its remaining BP shares in 1987.

The creation of the OSC in December 2022 is itself an explicit acknowledgement that capital allocation is becoming as strategically important as troop deployment. That’s why rather than rebel against the state-capitalism trend, investors, both in the UK and the US, would be better off recognising the value of joining in with patriotic investment flows.

Brent Johnson of Santiago Capital is among investors already doing so.

In a report published last year, he advised that the OSC’s published list of priorities should be viewed as an investment roadmap with the Pentagon’s list of target sectors acting as a “strategic map showing where the United States is most vulnerable and where private capital has underinvested relative to national security needs”.

The OSC’s job in that context is to “reduce risk for private investors” and crowd-in capital into those areas.

For investors, the signal could hardly be clearer: when the world’s most powerful government tells you which industries it considers indispensable to national survival, it may pay to listen.

This, however, is not just because we are going to see much more government involvement in markets as geopolitical fragmentation intensifies, it is because the comforting idea that Anglo-American capitalism ever operated entirely free of state direction was itself a misdirection. Especially when you consider the broader Western European context.

Even under the auspices of a supposedly free-market-championing EU, there has been far less anxiety in the Continent about displaying these dirigiste tendencies openly.

France, most obviously, has retained stakes in strategically important companies and industries from aerospace to energy. But even Brussels is now becoming more explicit, with Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, seeking to mobilise Europe’s vast pool of private savings into strategic sectors such as defence, while simultaneously pushing for greater European preference in strategic procurement.

That’s why, in Johnson’s view, it is better to understand the rise of the OSC, and its growing proximity to Wall Street, as the subtle unveiling of a “21st-century Manhattan Project” that has been operating in the background for some time. Its intent? To ensure that – when the time comes – private capital can and will be mobilised to finance the capabilities needed to compete with authoritarian challengers, both militarily and industrially.

Indeed, it’s also arguably why long before the OSC ever existed, there was In-Q-Tel. The CIA-backed venture was founded in 1999 and is behind technology superpowers like Palantir. Its creation arguably marked the moment the national-security establishment fully realised that innovation, particularly in information technology, would require the sort of commercial scale and private capital that could not be replicated behind classified walls.

To maintain its edge, government would need to seed the strategic capabilities it might one day need to draw increasingly in plain sight.

The OSC is the logical extension of that strategy.

Britain’s own versions of this machinery, the National Security Strategic Investment Fund and Advanced Research and Invention Agency, did not arrive until 2018 and 2023 respectively. They have, consequently, had far less time to shape the investment landscape.

But since the structures are now in place and their purpose is becoming clearer, investors should no longer delay getting on board. Putting capital behind the technologies and industrial capacity that defend the strategic autonomy of Britain and its allies is no longer merely patriotic. It is where governments themselves are telling us the money will flow.

data.title: CrossCountry cancels almost all trains after power cut
data.description:
CrossCountry has cancelled almost all its trains after a power cut at its Birmingham headquarters.

The long-distance rail operator warned of “significant disruption” on Sunday and said that services “across almost all routes will be withdrawn until further notice”.

The Birmingham city centre power cut has disrupted operations at CrossCountry’s main control centre, meaning systems used to manage its trains are unavailable.

The only CrossCountry route still running is between Peterborough and Stansted airport, calling at March, Ely and Cambridge.

CrossCountry tickets are being accepted via any reasonable route on all other train companies’ services, according to National Rail Enquiries. A normal service is expected to run on Monday.

A spokesman for CrossCountry said: “A power cut in Birmingham city centre has affected the building where our control centre is located. As a result, many of the systems our control teams use to manage the railway are currently unavailable.

“Although colleagues are working hard to safely operate services using alternative processes, CrossCountry services will be significantly disrupted on Sunday Aug 23.

“While we will run as many trains as possible, passengers should expect significant reductions to services and cancellations across almost all routes throughout the day. We are sorry to passengers affected by this significant and unforeseen disruption.

The National Grid operates the electricity distribution network serving Birmingham city centre.

On Aug 7, a similar power cut in Manchester caused a power cut at a Network Rail signalling control centre, leading to chaos across the north-west of England as all trains came to a standstill as a safety precaution.

The incident was triggered by a fault at a transformer in Ardwick, which provides energy for Network Rail’s Manchester Rail Operating Centre.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, said: “I am concerned to hear about a power outage affecting CrossCountry rail services, which I know will be very frustrating to passengers.

“I’ve asked publicly owned operators to lay on extra services where possible. We’ve also sent Network Rail power teams who are on-site and working to restore power and systems as soon as possible.”

A National Grid electricity distribution spokesman said on Sunday afternoon: “Our engineers are on site working to repair a fault affecting CrossCountry’s Birmingham control centre.

“We’re working closely with CrossCountry to restore power safely as soon as possible. We understand the frustration caused by disrupted journeys and are sorry for the inconvenience to passengers.”

Travellers delayed by more than half an hour are eligible to claim Delay Repay compensation from the train company via its website.

data.title: Currys’ turnaround king tasked with reviving tired Boots ahead of flotation
data.description:
When Currys announced that Alex Baldock, its chief executive, was stepping down earlier this year, the response from investors was immediate.

Shares in the electronics chain fell sharply – wiping almost 11pc off its valuation – as markets digested the departure of the man widely credited with engineering the company’s quietly successful turnaround.

Now Baldock appears poised for an even bigger challenge, tasked with reviving a 177-year-old brand that has seen better days. On Wednesday, it emerged that the outgoing Currys chief was being lined up to take the reins at Boots.

The company confirmed his appointment on Thursday, setting the stage for Baldock to try to convince investors that the British chemist could be worth as much as £7bn.

Baldock should be well-suited to the role. He has spent the past seven years proving that legacy retailers can still thrive if they modernise quickly enough.

At Currys, that meant slimming down the store estate, cutting costs, boosting online sales and emphasising its “omnichannel” offering of services, repairs, credit and subscriptions.

Adam Tomlinson, a retail analyst at Berenberg, says that when Baldock arrived at Currys in 2018, “the business was in a very tough place”.

“A major focus initially was restructuring the mobile division, which had become a significant drag on the wider group. He completely realigned it in terms of right-sizing both the store base and the cost base, and turned it from being a problem area into a positive contributor.”

Tomlinson says Baldock’s broader strategy has been to transform Currys from a “product-first retailer into an integrated services business”, encouraging customer loyalty through credit offers, delivery and installation, warranties, repairs and trade-ins.

“What is often overlooked is how much focus he placed on staff and colleagues,” he adds. “He has a mantra that customer experience can never exceed colleague experience.”

Baldock will now have to repeat that success at Boots – a brand which is desperately in need of a turnaround.

Since being folded into Walgreens Boots Alliance in 2014, Boots has endured closures, restructurings and repeated attempts to move away from its old-fashioned chemist image.

Its owners have repeatedly signalled that they would be keen to offload the British business. Walgreens launched a sale process for Boots in 2022.

However, it later scrapped the plans after failing to secure a deal at the valuation it wanted in the face of difficult market conditions and rising borrowing costs. Since then, efforts have been focused on honing the chain, including pushing through further store closures and cost reductions.

Speculation over a sell-off of the British arm was revived last year when private equity firm Sycamore Partners swooped to buy Walgreens Boots Alliance in a $10bn (£7.4bn) deal.

Shortly after the deal was completed, Sycamore split Walgreens into five standalone entities – one of which was Boots. It was seen as the first major step towards ultimately returning the British chemist to the UK stock market.

Baldock is believed by many to have been brought on to get Boots over the line for such a London listing – something insiders claim was “always the plan”. Its owners are looking for a valuation as high as £7bn. Still, some remain unconvinced that any listing would be imminent.

A senior retail industry source says his appointment is the same “as with any private equity-owned business”. “The job is to create as much value as possible for the owners,” the source says.

Given the current state of the London market, they say it is more likely that Baldock has simply been brought in to put Boots on a stronger footing. “I don’t think it’s right that he’s been brought in for an IPO.”

They say Boots’ health and beauty division is now “by far the most important part of the business”, reflecting the growing view inside retail that the future of Boots lies less in pharmacy and more in cosmetics, skincare and wellness.

That shift is already visible inside many of Boots’ larger stores, where beauty halls increasingly dominate the shop floor while traditional pharmacy space shrinks.

Boots has revamped more than 100 of its stores and updated beauty halls in more than 180 sites. It argues that this has helped it to record 20 consecutive quarters of market-share growth.

Analysts expect Baldock to continue pushing the business in the same direction because beauty products offer significantly stronger margins than dispensing medicines or selling low-cost healthcare essentials.

Jonathan De Mello, of JDM Retail, says Boots is “looking at devoting more floor space to beauty rather than distress pharmaceutical purchasing. The margins on beauty products are significantly better”.

At the same time, Boots still faces the challenge of balancing investment in physical stores with the need to boost online sales.

For all the investment Boots has poured into flagship stores and digital infrastructure, analysts argue the business still lags behind rivals on both fronts.

“The Advantage Card is strong, but the website still needs work,” says De Mello.

Former executives claim there are also still swathes of its sprawling estate which are in urgent need of investment. Renovating all of these old stores would be painfully expensive.

Clive Black, another retail analyst, agrees the chain’s estate remains uneven despite years of investment.

“There are some flagship stores where they have clearly invested heavily in beauty, but there are also an awful lot of stores around the country that look pretty tired,” says Black.

If Baldock wants to take Boots public – be it later this year or further down the line – he will have to convince investors that Boots can be a growth business rather than simply a reliable cash generator.

Black says he suspects that “Boots may end up being seen more as an income story than a pure growth story”.

Baldock will also inherit questions over Boots’ international operations.

While the retailer’s presence outside the UK may have formed part of the attraction for him personally – having steered Currys for years in both the UK and overseas – analysts suggest some international businesses could ultimately be sold off as management focuses more tightly on the chain’s strongest markets.

De Mello says Boots’ operations in places such as Germany and Mexico are underperforming. He argues the business would be better concentrating on the UK and Ireland, which he describes as the company’s “engine room for growth”.

At Currys, Baldock managed to convince the markets that physical stores still had value in the Amazon era, provided they worked seamlessly alongside a strong online offer. Between 2024 and 2026, he oversaw a tripling in the retailer’s share price.

Just last week, Baldock told The Times that he loved his role at Currys. His next move would have to be “something properly exciting to take me away from Currys”. With Boots, it seems that Baldock has found that. Now, he said, marked the start of “an exciting new chapter for Boots”.

data.title: Boots in £7.5bn sale talks with billionaire family behind Primark
data.description:
Boots is in talks to sell itself for £7.5bn to the family behind Primark and an Australian pharmacy chain.

The billionaire Weston family, which owns Primark, is weighing up a bid that would see the chemist scrap plans for a London listing, according to the Financial Times.

The retail giant is understood to be in talks alongside Sigma Healthcare, an Australian pharmacy group, about a possible takeover of the 177-year-old chemist from Sycamore Partners, its private equity owner.

A takeover of Boots would derail plans for a stock market listing. The recent appointment of Alex Baldock – the former Currys boss credited with turning around the electronics retailer – as chief executive had fuelled speculation that Boots was being prepared to join the London Stock Market. 

Insiders had previously suggested that a flotation valuing the chain at up to £7bn was “always the plan”.

News of the talks came as Boots revealed that profits jumped by a quarter to £337m last year, as demand for weight-loss jabs, vaccinations and beauty products helped drive sales growth.

The Westons are one of the world’s richest retail families. Through their sprawling business empire they already control Primark-owner Associated British Foods (ABF), as well as Fortnum & Mason and major supermarket and pharmacy chains in Canada.

A deal would also deepen the family’s ties to British retail just months after it unveiled plans to split Primark from ABF, ending a six-decade partnership between the fashion chain and the conglomerate’s food operations.

Sigma, meanwhile, is a fast-growing Australian healthcare group best known for its links to Chemist Warehouse, Australia’s largest pharmacy retailer.

It has recently signalled ambitions to expand internationally and only last month entered the UK market through a pharmacy joint venture in and around London.

Hundreds of stores closed

A sale of Boots has been talked about for years. Walgreens first tried to offload it in 2022, before abandoning the effort when bids failed to meet expectations.

Sycamore Partners revived expectations of a breakup when it bought Walgreens Boots Alliance last year and carved out Boots as a standalone unit.

Boots has spent the past two years trying to improve its attractiveness to potential bidders. 

It has closed hundreds of under-performing UK stores as part of a broader cost-cutting drive, including a programme to shut branches, trimming its footprint from about 2,200 stores to roughly 1,900 in 2024.

At the same time, the chain has benefited from a boom in private healthcare services and a push into premium beauty brands, with online sales also rising sharply as more shoppers turned to its app and delivery partnerships.

The Weston family already has a presence in the pharmacy sector through Shoppers Drug Mart, a Canadian chain with more than 1,300 locations that it acquired in a multibillion-pound deal more than a decade ago.

Boots declined to comment.

data.title: Britain’s gas cliff-edge is drawing dangerously close
data.description:
“Britain will control its own energy rather than depending on markets controlled by petrostates and dictators,” said Ed Miliband just before Labour won the 2024 election.

He was pledging to break the growing grip of countries ranging from Norway and the US to Qatar and Algeria on Britain’s energy supplies. Labour promised to replace imported oil and gas with low-carbon alternatives such as nuclear power, wind farms and solar plants.

Two years later, Britain faces a cliff edge in gas supplies, surging prices and soaring imports. This winter looks bad enough. Centrica’s Rough facility, the UK’s only major gas store, is facing the threat of closure without government support, and European storage levels are at their lowest in years.

Analysts are warning of January price increases on top of the 4pc increase planned in October and the 13pc rise last July.

But in a few years, they warn, the situation could be far worse because the UK’s North Sea output is plummeting faster than ever expected.

Last year the North Sea produced 28 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas – 41pc of Britain’s needs. But in four years, that will have halved to just 14 bcm. And by 2035 it will more than halve again, to 6 bcm.

That reduction could be mitigated by approving new fields such as Jackdaw and Rosebank – but not by much. And those raw figures, from the North Sea Transition Authority, the government regulator, are increasingly striking fear into the gas industry, energy suppliers and government ministers.

They imply that the UK faces increasingly tough, expensive and potentially cold winters over the next decade, and that Britain’s reliance on petrostates will be greater than ever.

“The gap between demand and supply is widening, and it’s going to widen even further in the coming years,” said Iryna Sereda, the global head of gas and LNG at BloombergNEF. “In 10 years, two thirds of the UK’s gas production will be gone.

“Demand is falling too, but not nearly so fast, which means the UK will become increasingly dependent on imports.

“By 2030 it’s likely to be above 70pc and by 2035, we could be as high as 85pc dependent on imports.”

That growing gap between North Sea supplies and UK demand will have to be filled. The only way to do that is by liquefied natural gas (LNG), all of which will have to be imported.

The US is Britain’s main supplier of LNG, but we also buy increasing amounts from Qatar, Egypt, Algeria, China, Equatorial Guinea and Turkey – all of them authoritarian states. And last year alone LNG imports rose 24pc.

So as North Sea output declines, the UK’s hopes of breaking away from “petrostates and dictators” look likely to go into reverse. How did a country that was once self-reliant in energy end up in such a mess? And have ministers even realised?

Gas stockpile plans

One sign that they are waking up came last month when it emerged that Miatta Fahnbulleh, the new Energy Secretary, is considering plans to acquire a large ship that would become the UK’s newest LNG import terminal.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero also confirmed plans to create a government-controlled stockpile of natural gas that could be drawn on in emergencies.

Both schemes recognise that the Government’s plans to reduce our reliance on gas are faltering, leaving the UK at increasing risk of price spikes and shortages.

Recently published North Sea Transition Authority data show the physical reality of the North Sea decline.

The UK has about 172 offshore gas fields operating in 2026, but by 2030 around 62 are scheduled to close, leaving just 110. By 2035, another 40 will be gone.

Some of that decline is natural. The North Sea is a mature basin, and output was gently falling by about 5pc a year up until 2022.

But after Rishi Sunak’s government adopted Miliband’s policy of a windfall tax, the annual decline surged to around 15pc as offshore operators scrambled to quit the North Sea.

That could get even worse. If, for example, John Healey carries out his threat to extend the windfall tax, many more North Sea fields would become uneconomic and shut down.

But it’s not just the UK’s own North Sea decline that it should be worrying about.

‘Norway is vital’

Norway, the supplier of about a third of the UK’s gas, is facing the same problem of natural decline.

Britain’s gas needs are not constant. They rise and fall with the seasons. But in the winter, when demand is highest, up to 90pc of the gas burnt in the UK is Norwegian.

That reliance is becoming a problem. A report from the Norwegian Offshore Directorate warns that Norway’s oil and gas supplies peaked last year at around 230 bcm and are expected to plummet to as low as 110 million cubic metres by 2035.

Nikolai Astrup, a Norwegian MP and a key figure on its parliament’s finance committee, said the UK should already be looking for new energy sources. He says: “Right now, Norway is Europe’s largest and most predictable supplier of gas, and all the gas and oil we produce is sold to the UK and Europe. Norway is therefore vital to European energy security.

“But it is a geological fact that the Norwegian Shelf is mature and that the fall in production will be very sharp from 2035 onwards.”

One solution is to reduce demand – an approach recommended by Seb Kennedy, of market data specialist Energy Flux. He argues that building more LNG import facilities would make the UK unhealthily reliant on imports.

He says: “Rather than expanding LNG import facilities, the UK should focus on measures that reduce demand, such as fast-tracking heat pump deployment, investing in heat networks and supporting homeowners with insulation costs.”

That sounds like a solution – until you look at the latest government data. Forecasts of falling gas demand are based on householders installing 600,000 heat pumps a year, mostly to replace old boilers.

But the reality is that 125,000 heat pumps were sold per year, only 7pc of the heating market, dwarfed by the 1.7 million gas and oil boilers purchased.

Gas consumption has fallen in other areas – but not necessarily in ways that benefit Britain. Industrial consumption has plummeted from 19 bcm in 2000 to 8 bcm last year – linked to the closure of thousands of factories.

But the reductions in demand from those shutdowns – and the corresponding displacement of gas-fired power generation by renewables – are nowhere near as fast as the looming decline in UK and Norwegian supplies.

‘Increasingly fragile’

ICIS, a commodity-market consultancy, has modelled the risks posed by this growing gas supply and warns that the winter of 2028-29 is when the threat could become real.

Organisations such as the National Energy System Operator always point to the UK’s diverse gas-supply sources as its best defences.

Those sources include North Sea output, piped imports from Norway, three LNG terminals, interconnector pipelines with Belgium and the Netherlands, and storage.

But ICIS analysis points out that with three of those sources in decline – the North Sea, Norway and storage – the UK is at increasing risk.

“Great Britain’s and Ireland’s security of gas supply becomes increasingly fragile under a declining trajectory of UK natural gas production,” it says.

“Under normal conditions, peak demand can be met, with spare capacity remaining ... In reality, however, each supply source is exposed to planned and unplanned outages.

“The loss of Norwegian imports, or the shutdown of either of the UK’s two large LNG terminals (Isle of Grain or South Hook) significantly reduces available supply.

“If this happens, supply fails to meet demand, not only on the peak demand day but also on multiple days across both the 2028-2029 winter and the preceding winter.”

Some experts say the UK’s and Norway’s decline in gas production matters little because global LNG supplies are growing fast enough to replace it.

David Luff, of Argus Media, said: “Over the next five years, UK gas production is expected to decline faster than consumption, increasing the reliance on imports. But this import dependence will coincide with a significant expansion in global LNG supply, driven primarily by new export capacity in North America and Qatar.”

“Ofgem backs that up. LNG imports will play an important balancing role, although competition for cargoes could intensify if global markets tighten,” said a spokesman.

In other words, far from breaking free from petrostates, Britain will become increasingly reliant on them.

Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said the growing reliance on imported energy was exactly the opposite of what the Government had promised before the election.

“The UK cannot continue to refuse to produce our own energy,” he says. “Labour’s ban on new licences, the windfall tax and delays in approving new fields like Jackdaw and Rosebank have put our energy security at risk. We need to get Britain drilling again.”
